must_mention: introduced in 2014 for long range dependencies
decoder peeks at relevant source words

followups.q: What was the bottleneck in an RNN encoder decoder?
followups.a: The whole source sentence had to fit in one fixed size hidden state.

followups.q: What did the 2017 paper change?
followups.a: It removed recurrence and used self attention so every token connects directly to all the others.

topic: CME295 L1: Transformer foundations
q: Explain queries, keys and values in attention with an intuition.
plain: Attention is a soft lookup: a query asks, keys describe what each token offers, and values hold the content. You compare the query with every key to get a similarity score for each token. A softmax (a function that turns scores into weights that add up to 1) converts the scores into weights. The result is the weighted sum of the values, so more similar tokens contribute more. The query, keys and values are all made from the token vectors by projections (matrix multiplications) that the model learns. For example, weights 0.7, 0.2 and 0.1 mix 70, 20 and 10 percent of three value vectors. Nobody sets the keys and values by hand, because the projections are learned during training.
deep:
Intuition from the lecture: to express the token teddy bear in terms of the other tokens, take its query and compare it to the key of every token. Tokens whose keys are more similar get larger weights, and the output is the weighted combination of their values.

Roles: the key is there so the query can find the most similar elements, and the value is the content associated with that element. The weight on each value comes from the query key dot product (after scaling and a softmax). Keys and values are learned projections of the same embeddings, not fixed in advance:

$$
Q=XW^Q,\qquad K=XW^K,\qquad V=XW^V
$$

For a whole sequence all of this is written as matrix products, which GPUs run efficiently. This soft lookup is a differentiable version of a dictionary access: a hard lookup returns one value for an exact key match, while attention returns a blend over all values.
say: I think of attention as a soft dictionary lookup. The query is what a token is asking for, the keys describe what each token offers, and the values are the content to retrieve. I compare the query with every key to get similarity scores, run a softmax to turn them into weights, and return the weighted sum of the values. So more similar tokens contribute more. All three are produced from the token embeddings by learned projection matrices, so nobody designs them by hand. For example, the query for teddy bear can pull in information from cute and reading.
must_mention: query asks, key matches, value is the content
output is the weighted sum of values
Q, K and V come from learned projections

followups.q: Why is it called a soft lookup?
followups.a: A hard lookup returns one value for an exact key. Attention returns a blend of all values, weighted by similarity, and stays differentiable.

followups.q: Are the keys and values fixed?
followups.a: No. They are learned linear projections of the token embeddings.

traps: Describing keys and values as pre defined features. They are learned projections.

topic: CME295 L1: Transformer foundations
q: Write the scaled dot product attention formula and say what each step does.
plain: Attention scores every pair of tokens with queries and keys, turns scores into weights, then mixes the values. Step one takes the dot product (multiply matching numbers, then add) of every query with every key. That gives one score per pair of tokens, so 5 tokens give a 5 by 5 table of 25 scores. Step two divides each score by the square root of the key size, which keeps the numbers from getting too large. Step three applies a softmax to each row, so each token gets weights that add up to 1. Step four multiplies those weights by the values, giving each token a weighted average of the value vectors. All of this is a few matrix multiplications, which graphics processing units (GPUs) run very fast.
deep:
$$
\mathrm{Attention}(Q,K,V)=\mathrm{softmax}\!\Big(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\Big)V,\qquad Q=XW^Q,\; K=XW^K,\; V=XW^V
$$

Shapes: $X\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_{model}}$, $W^Q,W^K\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{model}\times d_k}$, $W^V\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{model}\times d_v}$. Then $QK^\top\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$: row $i$ holds query $i$ against all keys (queries and keys must share the dimension $d_k$). The softmax is applied row wise, and the output is $n\times d_v$.

Small check (run with numpy): $Q=K=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$, $d_k=2$. The scaled score row for token 1 is $(0.707,0,0.707)$ and its softmax row is $(0.401,0.198,0.401)$.

Cost: time $O(n^2 d)$ and memory $O(n^2)$ for the score matrix, so the cost is quadratic in sequence length. Efficiency tricks such as sparse attention and KV caching come in Lectures 2 and 3.
say: Attention is softmax of Q times K transpose, divided by the square root of the key dimension, all times V. Q K transpose gives one score for every pair of tokens, so with n tokens it's an n by n table. Dividing by the square root of the key size keeps the scores in a reasonable range. The softmax over each row turns scores into weights that sum to one, and multiplying by V gives each token a weighted average of the values. It's all matrix multiplication, which GPUs do fast. The cost is quadratic in sequence length because of that n by n table.
must_mention: softmax of Q K transpose over square root of d k, times V
row wise softmax gives weights summing to one
multiplying by V mixes the values

followups.q: What are the shapes?
followups.a: X is n by d model, Q and K are n by d k, V is n by d v, scores are n by n and the output is n by d v.

followups.q: What is the time and memory cost?
followups.a: About n squared times d for time, and n squared for the score matrix, so it grows with the square of the sequence length.

traps: Applying the softmax over columns instead of rows. Each query row must sum to one.

topic: CME295 L1: Transformer foundations
q: Why does attention divide by the square root of the key dimension?
plain: Dividing by the square root of the key size stops the scores from growing too large as vectors get longer. A dot product adds up one product per dimension, so longer vectors give bigger sums. Big scores push the softmax (the step that turns scores into weights) to give one weight almost 1. In that case the slopes (gradients, or learning signals) of the softmax become tiny, and training stalls. Say each number is random with average 0 and spread 1. Then the dot product has a spread equal to the square root of the key size. With 64 dimensions the spread is 8, and dividing by 8 brings it back to 1. The weights stay soft enough for learning to continue.
deep:
Take $q,k\in\mathbb{R}^{d_k}$ with independent components of mean 0 and variance 1. Then $q\cdot k=\sum_{i=1}^{d_k}q_ik_i$ has mean 0 and variance $d_k$, so its standard deviation is $\sqrt{d_k}$. Dividing by $\sqrt{d_k}$ restores unit variance.

Simulation (100,000 random pairs): standard deviation of $q\cdot k$ is 2.0 for $d_k=4$, 8.0 for $d_k=64$ and 22.7 for $d_k=512$. After dividing by $\sqrt{d_k}$ all three are about 1.0.

Why it matters: when scores are large, the softmax saturates and its output approaches a one hot vector. The Jacobian of the softmax is $\mathrm{diag}(p)-pp^\top$, which tends to 0 as $p$ becomes one hot, so gradients flow back through the attention weights at almost zero rate and training stalls.

The lecture states it as: the dot products tend to grow as the dimensionality of the keys and queries increases, so normalize by the square root of the key dimension. The dot product requires $d_q=d_k$.
say: The dot product of a query and a key adds up one product per dimension, so its size grows with the key dimension. If the entries have mean zero and variance one, the dot product has variance d k, so its standard deviation is the square root of d k. Large scores push the softmax into saturation, where one weight is nearly one and the gradients are close to zero, so training stalls. Dividing by the square root of d k brings the variance back to about one. For d k of 64, that means dividing by 8.
must_mention: dot product variance grows with d k
standard deviation is the square root of d k

followups.q: What is the variance of the dot product of two random unit variance vectors?
followups.a: d k, since it is a sum of d k independent products each with variance 1.

followups.q: What happens to the softmax gradient when it saturates?
followups.a: Its Jacobian, diag of p minus p p transpose, goes to zero as p becomes one hot, so almost no gradient reaches the scores.

traps: Saying the scaling is only for numerical overflow. It mainly keeps the softmax out of the saturated, low gradient zone.

topic: CME295 L1: Transformer foundations
q: What is multi head attention, and why do the heads end up different?
plain: Multi head attention runs several attention computations side by side, each with its own learned projections. A head is one set of query, key and value projection matrices (tables of learned numbers). Each head can learn a different kind of link between tokens, much as a convolution layer uses many filters. The outputs of all heads are joined together and passed through one more matrix to return to the original size. The heads differ because nothing forces them to match, and training rewards using different views of the text. For example, 8 heads of size 64 are joined into 512 numbers per token, the size of the model dimension. The word head just means one copy of this attention computation, and the number of heads is written h.
deep:
Each head $i$ has its own projections $W_i^Q,W_i^K,W_i^V$ and computes attention in parallel. The outputs are concatenated column wise and projected by $W^O$ back to the embedding dimension:

$$
\mathrm{head}_i=\mathrm{Attention}(XW_i^Q,XW_i^K,XW_i^V),\qquad
\mathrm{MHA}(X)=\big[\mathrm{head}_1;\dots;\mathrm{head}_h\big]W^O
$$

Typical sizes: $d_k=d_v=d_{model}/h$, so the original model has $d_{model}=512$, $h=8$, $d_k=64$ and a total cost similar to one full size head.

Why the heads differ: nothing constrains them. The objective only rewards representations that help predict the right output, and gradient descent has no incentive to make several heads copy each other, so they converge to different projections. Random initialization also breaks the symmetry between heads (standard background). The lecture compares it to using multiple filters in a convolution in computer vision, and says papers exist that explore constraining the heads, but none is required.
say: Multi head attention runs several attention computations in parallel, each with its own learned query, key and value projections. The head outputs are concatenated and multiplied by an output matrix to return to the model dimension. Each head can specialise in a different kind of relationship between tokens, like using several filters in a convolution. Nothing forces them to differ, but they do in practice, because training rewards them for being useful rather than copies of each other. In the original model, eight heads of size sixty four are concatenated back into five hundred and twelve dimensions.
must_mention: parallel attention computations with separate projections
outputs concatenated then projected by W O
no constraint, gradient descent makes them differ
d k equals d model over h

followups.q: What does the output matrix W O do?
followups.a: It mixes the concatenated head outputs and projects them back to the model dimension.

followups.q: Does adding heads multiply the cost by h?
followups.a: No. Each head is smaller, with d k equal to d model over h, so the total cost is similar to one full size head.

traps: Claiming the heads are forced to specialize. They only tend to, because nothing rewards duplicates.

topic: CME295 L1: Transformer foundations
q: Describe the original encoder decoder transformer and what each part does.
plain: The original transformer has two stacks: an encoder that reads the input and a decoder that writes the output. Each encoder layer has self attention, where tokens look at each other, followed by a feed forward network. A feed forward network (a small two layer neural network applied to each token) adds more room to learn features. Each decoder layer has masked self attention, then cross attention to the encoder output, then a feed forward network. The encoder output is a set of context aware vectors, one per input token. Both stacks repeat the layer N times, and the original paper used 6 encoder and 6 decoder layers. At the end, a linear layer and a softmax turn the decoder output into probabilities over the vocabulary. Each layer keeps the shape: 10 tokens of size 512 go in and 10 tokens of size 512 come out.
deep:
Pipeline: tokenize, embed, add position information, run $N$ encoder layers, then decode with $N$ decoder layers, then a linear projection and softmax over the vocabulary.

- Encoder layer: multi head self attention, then a position wise feed forward network. Output: one context aware vector per input token.
- Decoder layer: masked multi head self attention over the output so far, then cross attention (queries from the decoder, keys and values from the final encoder output), then a feed forward network.
- Feed forward network: $\mathrm{FFN}(x)=W_2\,\mathrm{ReLU}(W_1x+b_1)+b_2$. Its hidden size is larger than $d_{model}$ (2048 against 512 in the original paper), unlike the narrow hidden layer of word2vec, to give the model more freedom to learn features.
- Each sublayer is wrapped in a residual connection and layer normalization (standard background, Lecture 2 covers normalization).

The final encoder output feeds the cross attention of every decoder layer. The original model used $N=6$, $d_{model}=512$ and $h=8$ heads. Because no layer changes the shape, an input of $n\times 512$ stays $n\times 512$ through the stack.
say: The original transformer is an encoder decoder model for translation. The encoder is a stack of layers, each with self attention and a feed forward network, and it produces a context aware vector for every input token. The decoder is also a stack, where each layer has masked self attention, cross attention over the encoder output, and a feed forward network. At the top, a linear layer and softmax give probabilities over the vocabulary. The original paper stacked six layers on each side. Each layer keeps the shape, so ten tokens of size five hundred and twelve in gives ten tokens of the same size out.
must_mention: encoder stack builds context aware token vectors
decoder: masked self attention, cross attention, feed forward
N stacked layers, 6 in the original
linear plus softmax over the vocabulary
final encoder output feeds every decoder layer

followups.q: Why is the feed forward hidden layer wider than the model dimension?
followups.a: To give the network more freedom to learn useful features. The original used 2048 against 512.

followups.q: Which encoder output goes into the decoder?
followups.a: The final encoder output is used as keys and values in the cross attention of every decoder layer.

topic: CME295 L1: Transformer foundations
q: Where do the queries, keys and values come from in encoder self attention, masked decoder self attention and cross attention?
plain: All three layers use the same attention formula, but they take their queries, keys and values from different places. In encoder self attention, all three come from the input tokens, and every token can see every other token. In decoder self attention, all three come from the output tokens written so far. It is masked (blocked), so a token cannot look at tokens to its right, which do not exist yet. In cross attention, the queries come from the decoder, while the keys and values come from the encoder output. So the decoder asks which input words matter for the word it is about to write. For example, at position 4 the decoder sees output positions 1 to 4 and all input tokens.
deep:
| Layer | Q from | K and V from | Mask |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Encoder self attention | input tokens | input tokens | none |
| Decoder masked self attention | output so far | output so far | causal |
| Decoder cross attention | decoder | final encoder output | none |

The lecture's quiz: of the three arrows into the cross attention layer, the one from the decoder is the query (what do I need to know about the input), and the two from the encoder are keys and values.

The causal mask adds $-\infty$ to the entries above the diagonal of $QK^\top$ before the softmax, so the weights on future positions are exactly zero:

$$
\mathrm{softmax}\Big(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}+M\Big)V,\qquad M_{ij}=\begin{cases}0 & j\le i\\ -\infty & j>i\end{cases}
$$

Cross attention gives an $m\times n$ weight matrix, with $m$ output positions and $n$ input positions. The mask also lets training process all output positions in parallel with their own prefixes (standard background), while generation still goes one token at a time.
say: The formula is the same, only the source of Q, K and V changes. In encoder self attention all three come from the input tokens, so every token sees every other. In decoder self attention they come from the output tokens so far, and a causal mask blocks tokens to the right, because those don't exist yet. In cross attention, the queries come from the decoder and the keys and values come from the encoder output, so the decoder asks which input words matter for the word it is about to write. The mask also lets training run all positions in parallel.
must_mention: encoder self attention: Q, K, V from input
decoder self attention is causally masked
cross attention: Q from decoder, K and V from encoder
mask sets future scores to minus infinity

followups.q: How is the causal mask implemented?
followups.a: Add minus infinity above the diagonal of the score matrix before the softmax, so future positions get zero weight.

followups.q: What shape is the cross attention weight matrix?
followups.a: Output length by input length, since each decoder position attends over all input positions.

traps: Saying cross attention takes queries from the encoder. The queries come from the decoder.

topic: CME295 L1: Transformer foundations
q: Why does a transformer need positional information, and how is it added?
plain: Self attention treats a sentence like a bag of tokens, because every token connects to every other one directly. Nothing in the formula says which token came first, unlike an RNN, which reads in order. So the model adds position information to each token's embedding. The original paper adds a pattern made of sine and cosine waves, one pattern for each position. Adding means element by element addition, so the result keeps the same size. Without it, dog bites man and man bites dog would give each word the same vector. For example, a 10 token sentence with embeddings of size 512 gets 10 position vectors of size 512 added in.
deep:
Self attention is permutation equivariant: shuffle the input tokens and the outputs are shuffled in the same way, with each token's output unchanged. An RNN gets order for free because it processes tokens one at a time. A transformer with direct connections does not, so order must be injected.

The original paper adds a sinusoidal position vector to each token embedding (same size $d_{model}$, element wise sum). With position $pos$ and dimension index $i$:

$$
PE_{(pos,2i)}=\sin\!\Big(\frac{pos}{10000^{2i/d_{model}}}\Big),\qquad PE_{(pos,2i+1)}=\cos\!\Big(\frac{pos}{10000^{2i/d_{model}}}\Big)
$$

The input matrix is then $n\times d_{model}$ with position built in. The lecture only mentions the sine and cosine convention. Lecture 2 covers sinusoidal embeddings in detail, plus learned embeddings, T5 bias, ALiBi and RoPE.
say: Self attention has no sense of order, because every token connects directly to every other and the formula never mentions position. Shuffle the tokens and each token's output stays the same. An RNN gets order for free by reading left to right, but a transformer doesn't, so I add position information to the embeddings. The original paper adds sine and cosine patterns of different frequencies, one vector per position, by element wise addition, so the size is unchanged. Without it, dog bites man and man bites dog would give each word identical vectors. Later lectures cover learned and rotary alternatives.
must_mention: attention has no built in order
RNN gets order from sequential reading
original paper uses sine and cosine
element wise sum keeps the shape

followups.q: What does permutation equivariant mean here?
followups.a: If you shuffle the input tokens, the outputs are shuffled the same way, so attention alone cannot tell the original order.

followups.q: Are positions concatenated or added?
followups.a: Added element wise in the original paper, so the dimension stays d model.

topic: CME295 L1: Transformer foundations
q: What is label smoothing and why does it help?
plain: Label smoothing changes the training target so the model is told the right word is likely, not certain. Many sentences have several good next words, such as what a wonderful day, lecture or book. A normal target is one hot, with 100 percent on the right word and 0 on all others. With label smoothing, the right word gets 1 minus epsilon, and the other words share epsilon equally. Epsilon is a small number you choose, such as 0.1. For example, with 10 words and epsilon 0.1, the right word gets 0.9 and each of the other 9 gets about 0.011. This makes the model less overconfident, and the transformer authors saw better scores on the bilingual evaluation understudy (BLEU) translation metric.
deep:
Instead of the one hot target $(1,0,\dots,0)$, use

$$
q_y=1-\varepsilon,\qquad q_k=\frac{\varepsilon}{V-1}\quad(k\ne y),\qquad L=-\sum_{k=1}^{V}q_k\log p_k
$$

with vocabulary size $V$. Check: with $V=10$ and $\varepsilon=0.1$ the targets are 0.9 and nine values of $0.1/9=0.0111$, which sum to 1.

Motivation from the lecture: in language there is usually more than one valid continuation, so asking for 100 percent on one word is too strict. It makes the model less confident and, in the original transformer paper, improved BLEU on translation. That paper also notes that it hurts perplexity, because the model is trained to be less sure.

Important detail from the Q and A: the softmax does not do this for you. You change the label that the prediction is compared against, not the output layer. Some implementations spread $\varepsilon/V$ over all words including the true one, which is a minor variant.
say: Label smoothing softens the training target. Instead of one hot, with a hundred percent on the right word, the right word gets one minus epsilon and the remaining epsilon is shared among the other words. With epsilon of 0.1 and a ten word vocabulary, the right word gets 0.9 and each other word about 0.011. It reflects that many sentences have several good continuations, and it stops the model becoming overconfident. The transformer authors reported better translation scores, though they noted it hurts perplexity, since the model is deliberately less sure.
must_mention: epsilon shared among the other words
changes the label, not the softmax

followups.q: Where is label smoothing applied?
followups.a: In the target distribution of the loss. The softmax output layer is unchanged.

followups.q: What trade off did the original paper report?
followups.a: Better BLEU and accuracy but worse perplexity, because the model is deliberately less certain.

topic: CME295 L1: Transformer foundations
q: Walk through how the transformer translates a sentence such as a cute teddy bear is reading, from start to end.
plain: First the text is split into tokens, plus a beginning of sequence (BOS) and an end of sequence (EOS) marker. Each token becomes an embedding, and a position pattern is added, giving a matrix with one row per token. The encoder stack turns this matrix into context aware vectors, one per input token. The decoder starts with only the BOS token and predicts the first word of the translation. It adds the predicted token to its input and predicts again, using masked self attention and cross attention. A final linear layer and softmax give a probability for every word in the vocabulary. This repeats until the model produces EOS, so a 6 token translation needs 7 steps, counting the EOS step. The encoder runs once, but the decoder runs once for every output token.
deep:
Steps (shapes in brackets):

1. Tokenize, add BOS and EOS markers, and look up learned embeddings ($n\times d_{model}$).
2. Add positional embeddings (sines and cosines in the original paper).
3. Run $N$ encoder layers: project to $Q,K,V$ with learned $W^Q,W^K,W^V$, compute $\mathrm{softmax}(QK^\top/\sqrt{d_k})V$ per head, concatenate heads, project with $W^O$, apply the feed forward network. Output: one context aware vector per input token.
4. Start the decoder with BOS. Each of its $N$ layers applies causal self attention, cross attention with queries from the decoder and keys and values from the final encoder output, then a feed forward network.
5. A linear projection and softmax give a distribution over the vocabulary. The chosen token (greedy or sampled, see Lecture 3) is appended to the decoder input.
6. Repeat until EOS is produced.

The decoder runs once per generated token, so a 6 token translation takes 7 decoder passes including the EOS step. Recomputing earlier positions at every step is wasteful, and the KV cache (Lecture 3) removes that redundancy. During training the whole target sequence is fed at once with the causal mask (teacher forcing, standard background).
say: I'd walk through it in order. Tokenize the sentence and add beginning and end markers, embed each token and add positional information, and run the matrix through the encoder stack to get a context aware vector per input token. The decoder starts with just the beginning token, applies masked self attention, then cross attention to the encoder output, then a feed forward network, and a linear layer with softmax gives next token probabilities. I pick a token, append it, and repeat until the end token appears. The encoder runs once, but the decoder runs once per output token.
must_mention: decoder generates one token per pass until EOS
linear plus softmax over the vocabulary

followups.q: When does generation stop?
followups.a: When the model produces the end of sequence token.

followups.q: How many decoder passes for a 6 token output?
followups.a: Seven, counting the pass that produces EOS, unless a KV cache avoids recomputation.

topic: CME295 L1: Transformer foundations
q: Why are transformers faster to train than RNNs and better at long range dependencies?
plain: A transformer handles all tokens at once, while a recurrent neural network (RNN) goes through them one by one. Self attention for a whole sequence is a few matrix multiplications, and graphics processing units (GPUs) are built for those. An RNN cannot compute step 50 before step 49, so its work cannot be spread across the GPU. In a transformer, any two tokens are connected directly, so the path between them is 1 step. In an RNN, a signal from token 1 to token 50 passes through 49 steps and may fade. The price is that attention compares every token with every other, so the cost grows with the square of the length. For example, 1,000 tokens means 1,000,000 scores per head and layer, while 2,000 tokens means 4,000,000.
deep:
| Property | Self attention | Recurrent layer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sequential operations per layer | $O(1)$ | $O(n)$ |
| Longest path between two tokens | $O(1)$ | $O(n)$ |
| Compute per layer | $O(n^2 d)$ | $O(n d^2)$ |

(The complexity row is the standard comparison from the transformer paper, not stated in the lecture.)

The lecture makes two points. First, self attention for the whole sequence is written in matrix form, and GPUs are built for matrices. Second, the direct connections between tokens address long term dependencies, as RNNs forget what happened far back because of vanishing gradients.

Parallelism is across positions during training. Generation is still one token at a time, because each new token depends on the previous one. The quadratic term is why efficiency work such as sparse attention (Lecture 2) and KV caching (Lecture 3) matters for long inputs.
say: Transformers train faster because they process all tokens at once. Self attention over a sequence is a few matrix multiplications, which GPUs handle very well, whereas an RNN must finish step 49 before step 50. Transformers are also better at long range dependencies because any two tokens are connected directly, one step apart, while an RNN passes information through every step in between and it fades. The price is quadratic cost in sequence length: a thousand tokens gives a million scores per head per layer. That memory and compute cost drives most of the efficiency tricks in later lectures.
must_mention: attention is matrix multiplication, GPU friendly

followups.q: Is generation also parallel across tokens?
followups.a: No. Training is parallel across positions, but generation produces one token at a time.

followups.q: What is the compute cost per layer for each?
followups.a: About n squared times d for self attention and n times d squared for a recurrent layer, so attention is costlier for very long sequences.

traps: Saying transformers are cheaper than RNNs per step. They are faster to train because of parallelism, but quadratic in length.

topic: CME295 L2: Transformer tricks and BERT
q: Why does a transformer need position embeddings, and how do learned and sinusoidal ones compare?
plain: Attention connects every token to every other token directly, so it cannot tell which token came first. A position embedding is a vector for each position, added to the token's own embedding. A learned version has a table of vectors that training adjusts, one row per position. Its limit is that it only knows positions seen in training, such as the first 512. A fixed version uses a formula based on sine and cosine waves, so nothing is learned. The formula works for any position, so it can run on longer text than training. For example, with 512 learned rows, position 600 has no vector, but the formula can still give one. The original authors tried both and found similar quality.
deep:
Self attention gives every token a direct link to all others, so unlike an RNN there is no sequential processing and the order of tokens is lost. Position must be injected. The original paper gives each position its own embedding of size $d_{model}$ and adds it to the token embedding.

Learned: a table $P\in\mathbb{R}^{L_{max}\times d_{model}}$ trained by gradient descent. BERT base has $512\times768=393{,}216$ such parameters. Drawbacks named in the lecture: it inherits biases of the training set (if something always happens at position 2, that gets baked in), and it only has vectors up to the longest training sequence, so a longer input at inference has no learned value.

Sinusoidal: a fixed formula with no parameters that works for any length. In the original paper both variants gave comparable quality, and the fixed one was preferred for its extension to any sequence length.

Both are added at the input, which is an indirect route to the attention scores. That is the motivation for relative methods inside attention (T5 bias, ALiBi, RoPE).
say: Attention treats tokens as a set, so position has to be injected. The simplest way is a learned embedding per position, added to the token embedding. It lets gradient descent do the work, but it only covers positions seen in training, say up to 512, and it can absorb biases of the training set. The alternative is a fixed sinusoidal formula that needs no training and gives a vector for any position, so it can extend past the training length. In the original paper, both gave comparable quality. Both are added at the input, which is why newer methods act inside the attention layer instead.
must_mention: learned: table limited to training length
both added to the token embedding
comparable quality in the original paper

followups.q: What happens to a learned table at a position beyond the training maximum?
followups.a: There is no learned vector for it, so you must infer or interpolate one, which hurts quality.

followups.q: Is position information concatenated or added?
followups.a: Added element wise, so the size stays d model.

traps: Saying sinusoidal embeddings are learned. They are a fixed formula.

topic: CME295 L2: Transformer tricks and BERT
q: How do sinusoidal position embeddings work, and why does the dot product of two of them depend on relative distance?
plain: Each position gets a vector made of sine and cosine values at many different speeds. Early dimensions wiggle fast, and later dimensions change slowly, like the second, minute and hour hands of a clock. A useful fact follows from a trig identity (a rule linking sine and cosine of two angles). The dot product of the vectors for two positions is a sum of cosines of the distance between them. So it depends only on how far apart the positions are, not on where they are. It is largest when the two positions are the same. For example, with 16 numbers per position, a position matched with itself scores 8. One step away it scores about 7.5, and 10 steps away about 3.6.
deep:
For position $m$ and pair index $i=0,\dots,d/2-1$:

$$
PE_{(m,2i)}=\sin(\omega_i m),\quad PE_{(m,2i+1)}=\cos(\omega_i m),\quad \omega_i=10000^{-2i/d_{model}}
$$

$d_{model}$ must match the token embedding size because the two are added. The dot product of two position vectors uses $\cos(a-b)=\cos a\cos b+\sin a\sin b$:

$$
PE_m\cdot PE_n=\sum_{i=0}^{d/2-1}\cos\big(\omega_i(m-n)\big)
$$

So the similarity is a function of $m-n$ only. At $m=n$ every term is $\cos 0=1$, the maximum, which equals $d/2$. This matches the intuition that nearby tokens should be more similar, and the dot product matters because cosine similarity is a normalized dot product. Cosines are periodic, so similarity is not strictly decreasing with distance.

Frequencies: low index $i$ gives a large $\omega_i$ (fast oscillation), high index gives a small one. For $d=512$, $\omega_0=1$ (wavelength $2\pi\approx6.3$ positions) and the smallest is about $10^{-4}$ (wavelength about 60,000).

Numerical check (run with numpy, $d=16$): $PE_{50}\cdot PE_{50}=8$, $PE_{50}\cdot PE_{49}=7.49$, $PE_{50}\cdot PE_{40}=3.65$.
say: Each position gets a vector of sines and cosines at different frequencies, low dimensions oscillating fast and high ones slowly, like clock hands. The nice property comes from the angle subtraction identity. The dot product of the vectors for two positions is a sum of cosines of their difference, so it depends only on the relative distance, and it is largest when the positions are equal. That matches the intuition that nearby tokens should be more similar. It's also a fixed formula, so it works for any sequence length. The caveat is that cosines are periodic, so similarity doesn't fall monotonically with distance.
must_mention: sine and cosine at different frequencies
dot product is a sum of cosines of m minus n

followups.q: Why do the frequencies differ by dimension?
followups.a: A range from fast to slow oscillation lets the vector encode both fine and coarse position, like clock hands of different speeds.

followups.q: Is similarity monotonic in distance?
followups.a: No. Cosines are periodic, so it can rise again at some distances.

traps: Claiming the dot product depends on absolute positions. It depends only on their difference.

topic: CME295 L2: Transformer tricks and BERT
q: Why do modern models inject position inside the attention layer, and how do the T5 bias and ALiBi do it?
plain: Attention is where tokens are compared, so position information works best when it enters the attention score directly. Adding it to the input only reaches attention indirectly. The T5 model (text to text transfer transformer) learns one bias per distance bucket, added to the score. Attention with linear biases (ALiBi) uses a fixed rule instead: the further apart two tokens are, the lower the score. A bias can be more negative for far apart tokens, so nearby tokens get more weight. Adding any number inside the softmax is fine, because the softmax rescales everything to add up to 1. For example, with a slope of 0.5, a token 4 steps away loses 2.0 from its score.
deep:
The property we want, that nearby tokens count as more similar, lives in the query key score, so the lecture argues position should act in the attention layer instead of being added at the input (where it only reaches attention indirectly). Add a bias term $B$ inside the softmax:

$$
\mathrm{softmax}\!\Big(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}+B\Big)V
$$

- T5: $B_{mn}=b_{\mathrm{bucket}(m-n)}$. Relative distances are grouped into buckets and one scalar per bucket is learned.
- ALiBi (Press et al., Train Short, Test Long): $B_{mn}=-s_h|m-n|$ with a fixed slope $s_h$ per head. Nothing is learned, so it can run on sequences longer than those seen in training.

A bias inside the softmax is allowed because the softmax normalizes the weights to sum to 1 anyway. Weaknesses named in the lecture: learned biases depend on the training set and can overfit, and ALiBi's simple formula of the distance is restrictive. Most models today use RoPE instead.
say: The similarity between tokens is computed in the attention score, so it makes sense to put position information there instead of at the input. T5 learns a bias per bucket of relative distance and adds it to the query key score before the softmax. ALiBi uses a fixed bias that gets more negative with distance, so there's nothing to learn. Adding a bias inside the softmax is fine because the softmax renormalizes. The trade offs are that learned biases can overfit the training set, and ALiBi's simple linear rule is restrictive, which is why most current models use rotary embeddings.
must_mention: position should act inside the attention score
T5: learned bias per distance bucket
ALiBi: fixed linear penalty on distance
softmax renormalizes so a bias is allowed

followups.q: Why is it fine to add a bias before the softmax?
followups.a: The softmax normalizes the outputs to sum to 1, so any additive term only changes the relative weights.

followups.q: What does ALiBi stand for?
followups.a: Attention with linear biases, from the Train Short, Test Long paper.

traps: Saying the bias is added after the softmax. It goes inside, before the softmax.

topic: CME295 L2: Transformer tricks and BERT
q: What is RoPE (rotary position embedding), and why do most modern models use it?
plain: Rotary position embedding (RoPE) marks position by rotating the query and key vectors by an angle that grows with position. A rotation is done by multiplying the vector with a small matrix of cosines and sines. Then the attention score depends on the two contents and on how far apart the positions are. Nothing is added to the input, so the position signal acts exactly where similarity is computed. It has no learned position parameters, and nearby tokens tend to score higher than far ones. For example, at 0.3 radians (an angle unit) per position, positions 2 and 5 turn by 0.6 and 1.5. Their difference, 0.9, depends only on the gap of 3 positions.
deep:
RoPE (RoFormer, Su et al.) rotates the query by an angle that is a function of its position $m$ and the key by an angle that is a function of its position $n$. In 2D the rotation is a multiplication by

$$
R(\theta)=\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta&-\sin\theta\\ \sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{pmatrix}
$$

and the query key product then contains a rotation by $(n-m)\theta$, so it depends on relative distance. For $d$ dimensions, split the vector into $d/2$ pairs and rotate pair $i$ by $m\theta_i$, with fixed frequencies $\theta_i$ that behave like the sinusoidal $\omega_i$ (a function of $i$ and $d$, not learned). Rotation is applied to $Q$ and $K$ only, not to $V$.

Why it is popular: it makes the position signal act inside the attention score like a relative bias, has no learned position parameters, and the RoFormer paper shows an upper bound on the attention weight that decays with distance (with some oscillation). The lecture notes that most models these days use RoPE and that the intuition is not obvious, which is why the sine and cosine picture helps.
say: RoPE, rotary position embedding, encodes position by rotating the query and key vectors by an angle proportional to their position. I rotate with a matrix of cosines and sines, applying it to queries and keys but not values. Then the dot product between a query and a key depends on their content and on the difference of their positions, so it's a relative encoding without adding anything to the input. It has no learned position parameters, and the attention bound tends to decay with distance. Most modern LLMs use it. In many dimensions, I split the vector into pairs and rotate each pair at its own frequency.
must_mention: rotate query and key by position dependent angles
rotation matrix of cosines and sines
applied to Q and K, not V

followups.q: Is theta learned?
followups.a: No. It is fixed, a function of the pair index and the dimension, roughly like the sinusoidal omega.

followups.q: Why not add position at the input instead?
followups.a: Adding at the input only reaches the attention scores indirectly. Rotating Q and K puts the relative position directly into the score.

traps: Saying RoPE rotates the values too. Only queries and keys are rotated.

topic: CME295 L2: Transformer tricks and BERT
q: Show that rotating a query by its position and a key by theirs makes the attention score depend on the relative position.
plain: Rotating two vectors changes the angle between them by the difference of the two rotations. Rotate the query by m steps and the key by n steps, each step being the same small angle. The dot product (the similarity score) depends on the angle between the two vectors. That angle has changed by n minus m steps, the gap between the positions. So the score depends on the gap, not on the absolute positions. For example, positions 2 and 5 give the same score as positions 100 and 103, since both gaps are 3. In many dimensions, the vector is split into pairs of numbers, and each pair is rotated by its own angle.
deep:
Step 1: a 2D rotation really rotates. Write $v=r(\cos\varphi,\sin\varphi)$. Then

$$
R(\theta)v=r\big(\cos\theta\cos\varphi-\sin\theta\sin\varphi,\ \sin\theta\cos\varphi+\cos\theta\sin\varphi\big)=r\big(\cos(\theta+\varphi),\sin(\theta+\varphi)\big)
$$

by the angle addition identities, so $R(\theta)$ rotates $v$ by $\theta$.

Step 2: use $R(a)^\top=R(-a)$ and $R(a)R(b)=R(a+b)$:

$$
\big(R(m\theta)q\big)^\top\big(R(n\theta)k\big)=q^\top R(m\theta)^\top R(n\theta)k=q^\top R\big((n-m)\theta\big)k
$$

The score depends on $q$, $k$ and $n-m$ only.

Numerical check (numpy, random 2D $q,k$, $\theta=0.3$): position pairs (2, 5), (12, 15) and (100, 103) all give $-0.02913$ to nine digits.

In $d$ dimensions the rotation is block diagonal with $d/2$ blocks, block $i$ using angle $\theta_i$ (fixed, roughly $\omega_i$). The lecture also cites the RoFormer appendix for an upper bound on the attention weight that decays with $n-m$.
say: In two dimensions, multiplying a vector by a rotation matrix with angle theta rotates it by theta, which follows from the angle addition identities for sine and cosine. If I rotate the query by m times theta and the key by n times theta, their dot product becomes the query transposed times the rotation by n minus m times theta times the key. That uses the facts that the transpose of a rotation is the opposite rotation, and that rotations compose by adding angles. So the score depends only on the difference n minus m. For d dimensions I rotate d over 2 pairs, each with its own fixed theta.
must_mention: transpose of a rotation is the inverse rotation
product becomes q transposed R of n minus m times k
blocks of two dimensions in d dimensions

followups.q: Why does the transpose of a rotation equal the inverse?
followups.a: A rotation matrix is orthogonal, and R of a transposed is R of minus a.

followups.q: How do you extend to d dimensions?
followups.a: Use a block diagonal matrix of d over 2 two dimensional rotations, each with its own fixed angle.

topic: CME295 L2: Transformer tricks and BERT
q: What does layer normalization do in a transformer, and what are gamma and beta?
plain: Layer normalization rescales each token's vector so its numbers have an average of 0 and a typical size of 1. It subtracts the average of the vector's numbers and divides by their standard deviation (the typical spread). Without this, some layers produce huge values and others tiny ones, which makes learning slow and unstable. The model also learns gamma, which rescales, and beta, which shifts, so it can undo the effect. In the original transformer it sits in each add and norm box, after adding the sublayer's input and output. For example, the vector 2, 4, 6, 8 has average 5 and spread about 2.24. It becomes about minus 1.34, minus 0.45, 0.45 and 1.34.
deep:
$$
\mathrm{LN}(x)=\gamma\odot\frac{x-\mu}{\sqrt{\sigma^2+\epsilon}}+\beta
$$

$\mu$ and $\sigma^2$ are the mean and variance over the $d$ features of one token's vector, and $\gamma,\beta\in\mathbb{R}^d$ are learned. In the original transformer each add and norm box computes $\mathrm{LN}(x+\mathrm{Sublayer}(x))$ (post norm).

Why: activations can have extreme values in some components in some layers, and the weights are hard to learn if activations vary too much. Normalizing brings them into a stable range, improving training stability and convergence speed. The lecture names internal covariate shift as the term for this phenomenon.

Check: $x=(2,4,6,8)$ has $\mu=5$, $\sigma=\sqrt5=2.236$ and normalizes to $(-1.342,-0.447,0.447,1.342)$.
say: Layer normalization takes one token's vector, subtracts the mean of its components and divides by their standard deviation. Then it applies two learned vectors, gamma to rescale and beta to shift, so the network can undo the normalization where that's useful. The motivation is that activations can vary a lot between layers, and that makes the weights hard to train. Normalizing keeps them in a stable range, which improves stability and speeds convergence. In the original transformer it sits in the add and norm boxes after each sublayer. The statistics are per token over its features, not across the batch.
must_mention: subtract mean, divide by standard deviation
per token over the feature dimension
sits in the add and norm boxes

followups.q: What is normalized over what?
followups.a: Each token's vector over its own features, with mean and variance computed per token.

followups.q: Why learn gamma and beta?
followups.a: So the network can recover any scale or shift that is useful after normalizing.

topic: CME295 L2: Transformer tricks and BERT
q: How have normalization layers changed since the original transformer: pre norm versus post norm, and RMSNorm?
plain: Modern models normalize before each sublayer (pre norm) instead of after the addition (post norm). In post norm, the original design, you add the sublayer output to its input and then normalize the sum. In pre norm, you normalize the input, run the sublayer, then add the result to the original input. The sublayer is either the attention layer or the feed forward network. Models also swapped layer normalization for root mean square normalization (RMSNorm), which divides by the typical size of the numbers. RMSNorm skips the mean subtraction and the beta, so it has fewer parameters to learn. For example, 2, 4, 6, 8 has root mean square 5.48 and becomes 0.37, 0.73, 1.10, 1.46.
deep:
Placement of the norm (with $F$ the attention or feed forward sublayer):

$$
\text{post norm: } y=\mathrm{LN}\big(x+F(x)\big),\qquad \text{pre norm: } y=x+F\big(\mathrm{LN}(x)\big)
$$

The lecture says the original paper used post norm and nowadays pre norm is used. A common reason (standard background, not stated in the lecture) is that pre norm leaves an untouched residual path, which makes deep stacks easier to train.

RMSNorm drops the mean subtraction and the shift:

$$
\mathrm{RMSNorm}(x)=\gamma\odot\frac{x}{\mathrm{RMS}(x)},\qquad \mathrm{RMS}(x)=\sqrt{\tfrac1d\sum_{i=1}^{d}x_i^2+\epsilon}
$$

Only $\gamma$ is learned. The lecture says convergence is comparable to layer norm with fewer parameters, so it is a bit quicker.

Check: $x=(2,4,6,8)$ has $\mathrm{RMS}=\sqrt{30}=5.477$ and normalizes to $(0.365,0.730,1.095,1.461)$.
say: The original transformer used post norm: add the sublayer output to its input, then normalize the sum. Modern models use pre norm: normalize the input, run the sublayer, then add the result to the original input. They also replaced layer norm with RMSNorm, which just divides the vector by its root mean square and learns only the scale gamma, with no mean subtraction and no beta. Convergence is about the same, but it has fewer parameters and is a bit cheaper. For example, the vector two, four, six, eight has a root mean square of about 5.48. Pre norm also keeps a clean residual path, which helps deep stacks train.
must_mention: post norm: normalize after the residual sum
pre norm: normalize before the sublayer
RMSNorm divides by root mean square
only gamma is learned, no mean or beta

followups.q: What does the sublayer F stand for?
followups.a: Either the attention layer or the feed forward network.

followups.q: What does RMSNorm remove compared with layer norm?
followups.a: The mean subtraction and the learned shift beta, keeping only the scale.

traps: Saying pre norm normalizes the output of the block. It normalizes the input of each sublayer.

topic: CME295 L2: Transformer tricks and BERT
q: What is the difference between layer norm and batch norm, and why do transformers use layer norm?
plain: Batch normalization averages each feature across the examples in a batch, while layer normalization averages across one example's features. A batch is a group of examples processed together during training. With batch normalization, one example's result depends on which other examples share its batch. That can make training and use differ, because at use time the batch may be one example. Layer normalization needs only the example itself, so it behaves the same in training and use. This is one reason transformers use layer normalization, and it also tends to work better there. For example, with 32 vectors of size 512, batch normalization computes 512 averages over 32 values each. Layer normalization computes 32 averages over 512 values each.
deep:
Given a batch of $B$ token vectors of size $d$:

| | Batch norm | Layer norm |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Statistics over | the batch, per feature (B values) | the features of one vector (d values) |
| Number of means | $d$ | $B$ |
| Depends on other examples | yes | no |
| Train and inference | differ (running averages at inference) | identical |

The lecture's reasons for layer norm in transformers: empirically it works better, and batch norm makes you dependent on the batch, which can introduce differences between training and inference. Variable length sequences and small batches make batch statistics less reliable (standard background).

The intuition behind either is the same: keep activations in a stable range so that weights in every layer remain learnable.
say: Batch norm normalizes each feature across the examples in the batch, while layer norm normalizes across the features of a single example. Transformers use layer norm for two reasons. First, batch norm makes one example's output depend on the others in its batch, and at inference the batch may be a single example, so training and inference behave differently. Second, empirically layer norm just works better for these models, especially with variable length sequences. Layer norm needs only the example itself, so it's identical in training and serving. Both are trying to keep activations in a stable range so that training converges faster.
must_mention: batch norm: statistics across the batch
layer norm: statistics across features of one example
batch dependence causes train inference gap
layer norm works better for transformers

followups.q: What does batch norm need at inference time?
followups.a: Stored running averages of the statistics, since the batch at serving time may be tiny or a single example.

followups.q: Which dimension does each normalize over?
followups.a: Batch norm over the batch for each feature, layer norm over the features of each example.

traps: Saying layer norm normalizes across the batch. That is batch norm.

topic: CME295 L2: Transformer tricks and BERT
q: Why is full attention expensive, and how do sparse or sliding window attention reduce the cost?
plain: Full attention compares every token with every other token, so the work grows with the square of the length. Doubling the text length makes attention about four times more expensive. Sliding window attention lets each token look only at its neighbors within a fixed window. Many models mix layers: some use local windows and some use global attention over everything. Stacked layers still pass information far, because each layer extends how far a token can indirectly see. For example, with 8,192 tokens and a window of 1,024, scores drop from 67 million to 8.4 million. The pattern is like the receptive field (the region an output can see) of a convolution in computer vision.
deep:
The attention matrix is $n\times n$, so time and memory are $O(n^2)$, which hurts as $n$ grows. Approximations restrict which pairs interact.

- Longformer (2020) tried local windows. Restricting each token to a window of size $w$ costs $O(nw)$.
- Nowadays this is called sliding window attention. Models typically use local attention in some layers and global attention in others, interleaved, with no set recipe. Windows are on the order of thousands of tokens.
- Mistral uses sliding window attention at every layer. Information still travels far through depth: after $L$ layers a token can be influenced by tokens up to about $L\cdot w$ positions away, like the receptive field in a convolutional network (for example 10 layers with a window of 1,000 reach roughly 10,000 positions).

Numbers: $8192^2=67{,}108{,}864$ scores against $8192\times1024=8{,}388{,}608$, which is 8 times fewer (per head and layer).

Different from this approximation: exact attention can avoid materializing the full matrix using tiling, as in FlashAttention (Lecture 4). Sparse patterns change which scores exist, while tiling changes how they are computed.
say: Full attention compares every token with every other, so cost grows with the square of the sequence length. Sliding window attention restricts each token to a window of neighbors, which cuts the cost to roughly the sequence length times the window. With eight thousand tokens and a window of a thousand, that's eight times fewer scores. Many models mix local layers with a few global ones, and stacking local layers still lets information travel far, like the receptive field of a convolution. The trade off is that some long range interactions become indirect or lost, and there's no standard recipe for the mix.
must_mention: n squared cost of full attention
sliding window: attend to neighbors only
stacked layers widen the receptive field

followups.q: How far can information travel with a window w and L layers?
followups.a: Up to about L times w positions, because each layer extends the reach by one window.

followups.q: Is sliding window the same as FlashAttention?
followups.a: No. Sliding window changes which scores are computed, while FlashAttention computes the exact full attention without storing the whole matrix.

traps: Saying sliding window attention is exact. It is an approximation that drops far pairs.

topic: CME295 L2: Transformer tricks and BERT
q: Compare multi head attention, multi query attention and grouped query attention.
plain: These three differ in how many key and value projections the query heads share. In multi head attention (MHA), every head has its own query, key and value projection matrices. In multi query attention (MQA), all heads share a single set of key and value projections. In grouped query attention (GQA), heads are split into g groups, and each group shares one key and value set. GQA sits between the two, and recent models often use it. Sharing shrinks the memory kept during text generation, at a small risk of lower quality. With 32 heads, MHA keeps 32 key and value sets, GQA with 8 groups keeps 8, and MQA keeps 1.
deep:
Let $H$ be the number of query heads. Every variant keeps $H$ separate query projections. They differ in key and value projections:

| Variant | Key and value sets | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| MHA (multi head) | $H$ | every head has its own $W^Q,W^K,W^V$ |
| GQA (grouped query) | $G$ groups, group size $H/G$ | middle ground, common in recent models |
| MQA (multi query) | 1 | extreme sharing |

The reason is the key value cache used in generation (next lecture): it scales with the number of key value heads, so GQA with $G=8$ on $H=32$ makes it 4 times smaller and MQA 32 times smaller. The idea can be applied in any attention layer, but it matters most for the masked self attention of decoder only models.

How to choose (lecture): it is driven by performance, latency and cost, model size and input length. It is not straightforward, but many recent models share projection matrices and GQA is what you would typically see, though not for every model.
say: They differ in how many key and value projections the query heads share. In multi head attention every head has its own query, key and value projections. In multi query attention all heads share one key and value projection. Grouped query attention is the middle: heads are split into groups and each group shares one key and value set. The point is the key value cache at inference, which scales with the number of key value heads, so going from thirty two to eight makes it four times smaller. The price is a small quality risk, and many recent models choose grouped query attention.
must_mention: MHA: separate K and V per head
MQA: one K and V shared by all heads
GQA: K and V shared within g groups
motivation is key value cache memory

followups.q: What is the ratio of cache sizes for MHA and GQA with 32 heads and 8 groups?
followups.a: 4 to 1, since GQA stores 8 key value sets instead of 32.

followups.q: Which one do most recent models use?
followups.a: Grouped query attention is the typical choice, though not universal.

traps: Saying MQA shares the query projections. It shares keys and values.

topic: CME295 L2: Transformer tricks and BERT
q: Why do MQA and GQA share the key and value projections but keep separate query projections?
plain: Keys and values are stored and reread at every step of text generation, so sharing them saves the most memory. When a model writes a new word, that word's query is compared with the keys of all earlier words. The keys and values of earlier words never change, so they are saved in a key value cache (KV cache). The cache grows with the number of heads, layers and tokens. Queries are used once and thrown away, so sharing them would save no cache memory. Queries may also be better kept separate, because each head asks its own question. For example, take a 32 layer model, 8,192 tokens, 128 numbers per head and 2 bytes per number. With 32 key value heads the cache is 4 gigabytes, and with 8 it is 1 gigabyte.
deep:
During decoding, each new token attends to all previous tokens: its query is new each step, while the keys and values of earlier tokens are the same every step, so a key value cache stores them (Lecture 3). Size per sequence:

$$
\text{cache bytes}=2\cdot L\cdot n\cdot H_{kv}\cdot d_h\cdot b
$$

with the factor 2 for keys and values. For $L=32$, $n=8192$, $d_h=128$, $b=2$ (16 bit numbers): MHA with $H_{kv}=32$ gives $4{,}294{,}967{,}296$ bytes (4 GiB), GQA with $H_{kv}=8$ gives 1 GiB, MQA with $H_{kv}=1$ gives 0.125 GiB.

Queries are only needed for the current token, so sharing them saves no cache. The lecture also gives an intuition for keeping them separate: the query is what asks whether something is similar to another thing, so keeping per head query projections keeps diversity. It adds that people also simply try variants to see what works. The numbers here are an illustrative configuration, not a specific model.
say: During generation, each new token's query attends to the keys and values of every earlier token. Those keys and values never change, so they're cached, and that cache is what eats memory. Sharing key and value projections across heads shrinks the cache directly. A query is only used once for the current token and then discarded, so sharing queries would save no cache memory, and keeping them separate preserves the variety of questions the heads ask. As a rough example, with thirty two layers, eight thousand tokens and a hundred and twenty eight numbers per head, the cache is about four gigabytes with thirty two key value heads and one gigabyte with eight.
must_mention: each step attends to all earlier keys and values
cache size scales with key value heads
queries are used once, no cache to save

followups.q: What is the cache size formula?
followups.a: Two times layers times tokens times key value heads times head size times bytes per number.

followups.q: Does sharing keys and values change the query count?
followups.a: No. All H query heads remain, only the number of key and value sets drops.

topic: CME295 L2: Transformer tricks and BERT
q: What are the three transformer model families, and why did decoder only models win for LLMs?
plain: There are three families: encoder decoder, encoder only and decoder only. Encoder decoder models, like the original transformer, read an input and write a separate output. Encoder only models, such as bidirectional encoder representations from transformers (BERT), build vectors for tasks like classification. They cannot generate text. Decoder only models keep just the decoder and write text one token at a time. Today's large language models (LLMs) are decoder only, because next word prediction is the simplest task to scale. Compute turned out to be better spent on one decoder than on an encoder plus a decoder. For example, a decoder layer in the original design has 3 parts, but a decoder only layer has just 2.
deep:
| Family | Layers contain | Examples | Typical use |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Encoder decoder | encoder: self attention and feed forward; decoder: masked self attention, cross attention, feed forward | original transformer, T5 family | translation, text to text tasks |
| Encoder only | self attention (no mask) and feed forward | BERT, DistilBERT, RoBERTa | classification, sentiment, token labeling, embeddings |
| Decoder only | masked self attention and feed forward | modern LLMs | text generation, chat |

Removing the encoder removes the encoder embeddings that would feed cross attention, so the cross attention module disappears and each stacked decoder layer has masked self attention and a feed forward network.

Why decoder only won (lecture): the original hypothesis was that the encoder helps build the decoder's representation, but people realized the compute budget is best invested in the decoder only. Next word prediction is the simplest objective, easy to scale and generalize, and well aligned with being a helpful chatbot, whereas objectives such as T5's span corruption need corruption and are more bespoke. Decoder only models are the center of the following lectures.
say: There are three families. Encoder decoder models, like the original transformer, read an input and write a separate output. Encoder only models, like BERT, produce rich vectors for classification and token labeling, but they can't generate text. Decoder only models keep just the masked self attention and feed forward layers and generate one token at a time. Modern LLMs are decoder only because next word prediction is the simplest objective to scale, it needs no corruption or labels, and it matches what chatbots do. People found compute was better spent on a single decoder than split between an encoder and a decoder.
must_mention: encoder decoder: input in, separate output out
decoder only: masked self attention and feed forward
next word prediction is simple and scales
compute is better spent on one decoder

followups.q: What happens to cross attention in a decoder only model?
followups.a: It disappears, since there is no encoder output to attend to.

followups.q: Why not use an encoder only model for chat?
followups.a: It has no decoder, so it cannot generate text.

traps: Saying decoder only models are bidirectional. Their self attention is masked and causal.

topic: CME295 L2: Transformer tricks and BERT
q: What is T5's span corruption objective, and how does it differ from next token prediction?
plain: T5 stands for text to text transfer transformer, an encoder decoder model family. Instead of predicting the next word, it learns by filling in blanks. Parts of the input sentence are cut out and replaced by marker tokens called sentinels. The encoder reads the damaged sentence, and the decoder writes out the missing pieces in order. Each missing piece is introduced by its sentinel, and a final sentinel marks the end. For example, the input my teddy bear [gap 1] reading has the target [gap 1] is cute and [gap 2]. Variants include multilingual T5 (mT5) and ByT5, which reads raw bytes, giving a vocabulary of just 256.
deep:
The original transformer was trained for next token prediction. The T5 family trains with span corruption: pick one or more spans of the input, replace each with a sentinel token, and feed the corrupted text to the encoder. The decoder then outputs the sentinel for the first gap, the tokens of the missing span, the next sentinel, and so on, ending with one more sentinel, so $n$ corrupted spans give $n+1$ sentinels in the target.

Example. Text: my teddy bear is cute and reading. Encoder input: my teddy bear $\langle X\rangle$ reading. Decoder target: $\langle X\rangle$ is cute and $\langle Y\rangle$.

Training uses teacher forcing: the whole target is fed to the decoder at once and every position is predicted together (the lecture's description of the process).

Family: T5 (text to text transfer transformer), mT5 (multilingual, more work on the data and the vocabulary) and ByT5, a tokenizer free variant on bytes with a vocabulary of $2^8=256$ instead of about 30,000. Span corruption is more complex than next token prediction, which is part of why later LLMs use next token prediction.
say: T5 frames every task as text to text, and it trains with span corruption instead of next token prediction. I cut spans out of the input and replace each with a sentinel token. The encoder reads the damaged sentence, and the decoder outputs each sentinel followed by the missing tokens, ending with one more sentinel. So my teddy bear gap one reading has the target gap one is cute and gap two. Training uses teacher forcing, feeding the whole target at once. It was dropped by later LLMs because next word prediction is simpler to scale. Variants include mT5 for many languages and ByT5, which works on bytes.
must_mention: n spans give n plus 1 sentinels
more bespoke than next word prediction

followups.q: What is a sentinel token?
followups.a: A marker in the input that stands for a missing span, and in the target it introduces each reconstructed span.

followups.q: What is ByT5?
followups.a: A tokenizer free T5 variant working on bytes, with a vocabulary of 256.

topic: CME295 L2: Transformer tricks and BERT
q: What is BERT, and what does bidirectional mean compared with a decoder's causal attention?
plain: BERT stands for bidirectional encoder representations from transformers, and it is the encoder half of the transformer. It turns text into vectors that carry meaning from the whole input, ready for tasks like classification. Bidirectional means each token attends to tokens on both its left and its right. A decoder's masked attention is causal, so a token only sees itself and earlier tokens. BERT has no mask, so every token sees every other token. That helps understanding but rules out text generation, because there is no decoder. For example, in a 12 word sentence, each word sees all 11 other words, before and after it.
deep:
BERT (Devlin et al., 2018) is the encoder of the transformer with new training objectives. The self attention layers have no mask, so every token attends to every other token, and each output representation has attended to the whole input. This contrasts with the causal mask of a decoder, where a token attends only to itself and earlier tokens. The BERT paper stresses that GPT is not truly bidirectional while its encodings are.

Outputs are contextual embeddings: the vector for bank differs between a river sentence and a money sentence, unlike word2vec. They suit classification, sentiment and token labeling, and a small head is added on top. There is no decoder, so there is no text generation.

ELMo (embeddings from language models) came from the same period. It used stacked bidirectional LSTMs for contextual embeddings but was hard to scale because of recurrence, so BERT became the central model of this family.
say: BERT is the encoder half of the transformer, trained to build contextual embeddings. Bidirectional means every token attends to tokens on both sides, because there's no causal mask, whereas a decoder token only sees itself and earlier tokens. That makes BERT very good at understanding tasks like classification, sentiment and span extraction. The catch is that it has no decoder, so it can't generate text. For example, the word bank in a sentence gets a vector that reflects both the words before and after it, so a river bank and a money bank come out different, unlike word2vec.
must_mention: no mask: attends left and right

followups.q: How did ELMo differ?
followups.a: It used stacked bidirectional LSTMs, so it was contextual too but hard to scale because of recurrence.

followups.q: Why can't BERT generate text?
followups.a: It has no decoder and its attention sees the whole input, so it cannot produce tokens one at a time.

traps: Saying GPT style models are bidirectional. They use a causal mask.

topic: CME295 L2: Transformer tricks and BERT
q: What are the CLS, SEP and PAD tokens in BERT, and which three embeddings are summed at its input?
plain: BERT adds special tokens to the text, and each token's input vector is a sum of three embeddings. CLS (short for classification) goes first and ends up carrying a summary of the whole input. SEP (short for separator) marks the boundary between two sentences. PAD tokens fill the end of shorter inputs so every input in a batch has the same length. The three embeddings are the token embedding, a position embedding and a segment embedding. The segment embedding has only two values, A for the first sentence and B for the second. For example, an 8 token input padded to length 10 gets 2 PAD tokens.
deep:
Special tokens: CLS is a placeholder at the start of the sequence. After all attention layers its output is projected and used for classification, so it carries the bidirectional information of the whole input. SEP separates two sentences (used by the next sentence objective). PAD fills sequences to a fixed length, because training uses batches that are matrices of fixed length (an attention mask makes the model ignore them, standard background).

Input vector per token = token embedding (lookup table over a WordPiece vocabulary of about 30,000, the lecture's order of magnitude) + position embedding + segment embedding:

- Position: added as in the transformer. The lecture was unsure whether BERT used a fixed or learned version and notes the performance is similar. BERT learns them, with a maximum of 512 positions (standard background).
- Segment: new in BERT. Only two learned vectors, A for tokens of the first sentence and B for the second, the same vector for every token of a sentence. It was meant to help the next sentence task, though the lecture notes this hypothesis was challenged later.

Notation in the paper: $L$ layers (the transformer's $n$), $H$ the embedding size ($d_{model}$), $A$ heads ($h$). BERT base: $L=12$, $H=768$, $A=12$, about 110 million parameters (the large model has 24, 1024 and 16, standard background). Cased and uncased versions differ in whether the text was lowercased.
say: BERT's input has special tokens and a three part embedding. CLS goes first and its output vector acts as a summary of the whole input for classification. SEP separates two sentences. PAD tokens fill shorter inputs so a batch has fixed length. Each token's input vector is the sum of a token embedding from a WordPiece vocabulary of about thirty thousand, a position embedding, and a segment embedding that says whether the token is in sentence A or sentence B. The segment embedding was meant to help the next sentence task, though later work questioned whether it matters.
must_mention: CLS: placeholder that summarizes the input
PAD: fills batches to fixed length
token plus position plus segment embedding
segment A or B, two learned vectors

followups.q: How many distinct segment embeddings exist?
followups.a: Two, A and B, shared by all tokens of the same sentence.

followups.q: What tokenizer does BERT use?
followups.a: WordPiece, which learns merge rules that maximize likelihood, with a vocabulary of about 30,000.

traps: Thinking the segment embedding differs per token. It is the same vector for every token of a sentence.

topic: CME295 L2: Transformer tricks and BERT
q: How does masked language modeling work in BERT, including the 80, 10, 10 rule?
plain: Masked language modeling hides some tokens and trains the model to guess them from the words on both sides. Because it must use both left and right context, it learns bidirectional representations. A token chosen for prediction is replaced by a mask token 80 percent of the time. It is swapped for a random word 10 percent of the time, and left unchanged the other 10 percent. The model must predict the original token in all three cases. The standard recipe picks about 15 percent of tokens, so a 200 token text has about 30 targets. For example, of 100 chosen tokens, about 80 are masked, 10 are random words and 10 stay the same.
deep:
Masked language modeling (MLM) selects a subset of input tokens (about 15 percent in BERT, standard background) and trains the model to predict the original token at each selected position, with cross entropy over the vocabulary. The lecture's replacement rule for the selected tokens:

- 80 percent: replaced by the mask token.
- 10 percent: replaced by a random other token.
- 10 percent: left unchanged, and the model must still predict the same token.

Intuition from the lecture: to predict a token you need its context, so the model must learn what surrounds it on the left and on the right, which is the bidirectional property in action. The BERT paper's rationale for the random and unchanged cases (standard background) is that the mask token never appears at fine tuning time, so the model must keep a good representation for every token and cannot rely on seeing a mask.

MLM is unsupervised, since labels come from the text itself. Arithmetic: 15 percent of 200 tokens is 30 targets, of which about 24 become masks, 3 random words and 3 unchanged.
say: In masked language modeling I pick a subset of tokens, typically about fifteen percent, and train the model to predict the originals from the context on both sides. Of the chosen tokens, eighty percent are replaced by a mask token, ten percent by a random word, and ten percent are left unchanged. The model has to predict the original in all three cases. That forces it to use left and right context, which is what makes it bidirectional. The random and unchanged cases mean it can't rely on seeing a mask, since there are no mask tokens at fine tuning time.
must_mention: predict hidden tokens from both sides
80 percent mask, 10 percent random, 10 percent unchanged
labels come from the text itself

followups.q: Why leave some selected tokens unchanged or random?
followups.a: The mask token never appears at fine tuning, so the model must keep a good representation of every token and cannot depend on seeing a mask.

followups.q: Is MLM supervised?
followups.a: No. The labels are the original tokens, so it needs only unlabeled text.

traps: Saying every selected token is replaced by the mask. Only 80 percent are.

topic: CME295 L2: Transformer tricks and BERT
q: What is next sentence prediction in BERT, and was it needed?
plain: BERT (bidirectional encoder representations from transformers) is pretrained with two tasks, and next sentence prediction (NSP) is one. NSP is a yes or no task: do these two sentences follow each other in the text? Training pairs are built from a text collection, so labels come free. Half the time sentence B truly follows sentence A, and half the time B is a random sentence. A small classifier on top of the CLS vector predicts which case it is. The hope was that this teaches how sentences relate. Later work found it adds little, and the RoBERTa model (a retrained BERT) dropped it with almost no loss. For example, 1,000 training pairs would have about 500 true neighbors and 500 random pairs.
deep:
NSP builds an input of two sentences A and B joined by SEP. In 50 percent of examples B truly follows A in the corpus, and in the other 50 percent B is a random sentence. A classification head on the CLS output predicts whether A and B are consecutive (a binary cross entropy loss). The label is known because you control which sentences follow each other, so it is self supervised and needs no human labels. The segment embeddings A and B were introduced to help with this task.

It is still an encoder task: it is classification, not generation (a question raised in the lecture).

The authors assumed the combination of MLM and NSP helps learn general embeddings of high quality. The lecture lists as a limitation that it is unclear that both are needed, and RoBERTa then showed that removing NSP led to almost no decrease in performance.
say: Next sentence prediction is a binary classification task. I take two sentences, and half the time B truly follows A, and half the time B is a random sentence. A small classifier on top of the CLS output predicts which case it is. The labels come for free from the corpus, so it's self supervised. The hope was that it teaches how sentences relate, which helps tasks with sentence pairs. Later work, notably RoBERTa, found that dropping it costs almost nothing, so most newer encoders skip it. It's still an encoder task, since it's classification rather than generation.
must_mention: labels come free from the corpus

followups.q: Why is it still an encoder task?
followups.a: It is a classification on the CLS output, so no decoder or generation is involved.

followups.q: What did RoBERTa find?
followups.a: Removing NSP caused almost no loss in performance.

topic: CME295 L2: Transformer tricks and BERT
q: Describe BERT's two stage training, pretraining and fine tuning, with its strengths and weaknesses.
plain: These models are trained in two stages: pretraining first, then fine tuning. Pretraining learns general language skills from large amounts of unlabeled text.
