Its tasks are masked word guessing and next sentence prediction, and the labels come from the text itself. Fine tuning then adds a small layer on top and trains on a task with few labeled examples, such as sentiment. You can freeze the pretrained weights and train only the new layer, or retrain the whole network. Strength: little labeled data is needed, and results beat the best methods of the time. Weakness: it cannot generate text, and two stages are more work than a one shot method. For example, a sentiment model might need only 1,000 labeled reviews on top of pretraining on millions of unlabeled sentences.
deep:
Stage 1, pretraining: train the encoder on unlabeled text with two objectives, masked language modeling (learn the internal structure of the inputs) and next sentence prediction (check whether sentence order makes sense). Both are self supervised or unsupervised, since the labels come from the text.

Stage 2, fine tuning: keep the learned embeddings and weights and attach another network, typically a linear projection, then train for a target task such as sentiment classification (on the CLS output), token classification or question answering. You can freeze the pretrained weights and train only the small head, or retrain the whole network. The choice depends on how much of the network you are willing to retrain and how different the task is from pretraining.

Pros (lecture): pretraining uses abundant unlabeled data, then little labeled data is needed, and results exceeded the state of the art at the time. Cons: text generation tasks are out of reach without a decoder, and the two stage process can be heavier than a one shot method.
say: BERT trains in two stages. In pretraining, I train on lots of unlabeled text with masked language modeling and next sentence prediction, so the labels come from the text itself. In fine tuning, I keep the learned weights, add a small head such as a linear layer, and train on a labeled task, either freezing the base or updating everything. The strength is that I need little labeled data and it beat the best methods of its time. The weaknesses are that it can't generate text, and a two stage process is heavier than a one shot method.
must_mention: pretrain on unlabeled text with MLM and NSP
fine tune with a small head on labeled data

followups.q: When would you freeze the pretrained weights?
followups.a: When you want cheap training or the target task is close to the pretraining task. Retrain everything when you can afford it or the task differs a lot.

followups.q: What goes on top for sentiment?
followups.a: A linear layer or small network on the CLS output.

topic: CME295 L2: Transformer tricks and BERT
q: In BERT fine tuning for classification, why use only the CLS output, and how does question answering use the other tokens?
plain: The classification token (CLS) attends to every other token, so its output vector summarizes the whole input. For sentiment, the CLS output goes into a small network that predicts positive or negative. The other token outputs are simply ignored, because the task needs only one answer for the whole text. CLS is processed like any token, with its own query, key and value. Question answering needs a decision per token instead. Two small networks look at each token's output and predict where the answer starts and where it ends. For example, in a 100 token passage, the model picks a start position and an end position among 100.
deep:
CLS is embedded like any token, projected to its own query, key and value, and goes through the same attention layers, so its output has mixed in information from every other token and is context aware. For sentence level classification only this output is needed. It is passed to a small feed forward network, typically two matrices (a hidden layer and an output layer) mapping from the embedding size to the labels, for example positive or negative.

For token level tasks every output embedding is used. In question answering, two networks (heads) are applied to each token embedding to predict whether the token is the start of the answer and whether it is the end, a token level objective. The same pattern covers named entity recognition and other token classification.

So dropping the other embeddings is a convention for sentence classification, not a rule: which outputs you keep depends on the level of the task.
say: For sentence classification, I use only the CLS output. Because CLS goes through the same attention layers as every token, with its own query, key and value, its final vector has mixed in information from the whole input, so it works as a summary. I feed it to a small network, usually two matrices, that predicts the label. The other token outputs are ignored for that task. For token level tasks I use all of them. In question answering, two small heads read each token output and predict where the answer starts and where it ends.
must_mention: CLS output has attended to all tokens
small network on the CLS output
other outputs ignored for sentence tasks
token level tasks use every output
QA predicts answer start and end

followups.q: Does CLS get special attention treatment?
followups.a: No. It gets its own query, key and value like any token, and the same attention process.

followups.q: How would you do named entity recognition?
followups.a: Apply a classification head to every token output instead of only CLS.

topic: CME295 L2: Transformer tricks and BERT
q: What is knowledge distillation, and how does DistilBERT use it?
plain: Distillation trains a small student model to copy the output probabilities of a big teacher model. The probabilities, called soft targets, carry more knowledge than a single correct label. A teacher giving 70, 20 and 10 percent to three classes shows which wrong answers are close. The student matches the teacher by minimizing Kullback Leibler (KL) divergence, a measure of how different two distributions are. With a hard label as the teacher, this becomes the usual cross entropy loss. For example, teacher 0.7, 0.2, 0.1 against student 0.5, 0.3, 0.2 gives KL about 0.085, and training shrinks it. DistilBERT halves the layers of BERT (bidirectional encoder representations from transformers) and uses distillation to keep almost the same quality.
deep:
Idea (Hinton, Vinyals and Dean): the output distribution of a model shows what it has learned, so the soft targets contain almost all of the knowledge. In distillation a smaller student $S$ is trained to match the output distribution of a larger teacher $T$ rather than hard labels, minimizing the KL divergence:

$$
D_{KL}\big(y^T\,\|\,y^S\big)=\sum_k y^T_k\log\frac{y^T_k}{y^S_k}
$$

Reading it: in a world described by the teacher, how bad is it to model with the student. If the teacher is a hard label $y^T=e_c$, then $D_{KL}=-\log y^S_c$, which is the cross entropy loss.

Check: $y^T=(0.7,0.2,0.1)$, $y^S=(0.5,0.3,0.2)$ gives $0.7\ln1.4+0.2\ln0.667+0.1\ln0.5=0.0851$. A one hot teacher with the student giving 0.5 to the right class gives $-\ln0.5=0.693$.

DistilBERT (a short and impactful paper, as the lecture says): reducing the number of layers by two gives a lot of gains with almost the same performance, and distillation is used to retain that performance. I have left out the paper's headline percentages because the lecture did not state them.
say: Distillation trains a small student to imitate a large teacher. Instead of hard labels, the student matches the teacher's full output distribution, called soft targets, which carry more information, for example which wrong answers are close to right. The loss is KL divergence from the teacher to the student, and when the teacher is a one hot label it reduces to ordinary cross entropy. DistilBERT halved BERT's layers and used distillation to keep almost the same performance, with a much smaller and faster model. The cost is a separate training run, and the student is usually a little worse than the teacher.
must_mention: reduces to cross entropy for a hard label

followups.q: Why is KL divergence not symmetric, and which direction is used?
followups.a: It is not symmetric. Distillation uses the teacher distribution as the reference, so it measures the cost of modeling the teacher with the student.

followups.q: Why do soft targets help more than hard labels?
followups.a: They show relative similarity between classes, so the student learns more per example.

traps: Saying distillation uses only the teacher's top prediction. It uses the whole distribution.

topic: CME295 L2: Transformer tricks and BERT
q: What did RoBERTa change relative to BERT?
plain: RoBERTa keeps the architecture of BERT (bidirectional encoder representations from transformers) but trains it better. It drops the next sentence prediction task, because removing it hurt almost nothing. It uses dynamic masking, which picks new masked tokens each time the same text is seen. It also found that the original model was vastly undertrained, so it used much more and more varied data. Benchmark scores rose on the same tests. For example, over 10 epochs (passes over the data), each text can get 10 different masks. The lesson is that the training recipe matters as much as the design.
deep:
RoBERTa (Liu et al., 2019) keeps BERT's architecture and changes the recipe:

- Remove next sentence prediction: the study found no meaningful drop in performance without it.
- Dynamic masking: the masked positions are re-sampled every time a text is seen (for example at each epoch) instead of being fixed once, so one text yields many different masks.
- More and more diverse data: the original model was vastly undertrained, so RoBERTa raised the diversity and size of the data (and trained longer).

Benchmark performance went up quite a bit on the same benchmarks. The takeaways: some original design choices (the sentence order objective, and with it the segment embedding hypothesis) were not needed, and data and training budget matter as much as the architecture.
say: RoBERTa keeps BERT's architecture but fixes the training. It dropped next sentence prediction after finding it made almost no difference. It uses dynamic masking, choosing new masked tokens every time a text is seen, instead of masking once. And it found BERT was undertrained, so it used much more and more varied data and trained longer. Benchmark scores went up on the same tests. The lesson is that training recipe and data can matter as much as architecture, and that some of the original design choices, like the sentence order objective, weren't needed.

followups.q: What is dynamic masking?
followups.a: Choosing new masked positions every time a text is seen, rather than masking each text once in preprocessing.

followups.q: Did RoBERTa change the architecture?
followups.a: No. It kept BERT's architecture and changed the objectives and data.

topic: CME295 L2: Transformer tricks and BERT
q: What are BERT's main limitations, and how did later models address each?
plain: BERT (bidirectional encoder representations from transformers) has three main limits: short context, high cost and a complicated recipe. The original context length is 512 tokens, so long documents do not fit. Attention tricks such as local attention can extend the context without exploding the cost. BERT base has about 110 million parameters, which is slow and costly for many uses. DistilBERT shrinks it with distillation, using half the layers for nearly the same quality. Next sentence prediction and masked language modeling may not both be needed. RoBERTa dropped next sentence prediction and trained longer on more data. For example, a 3,000 token document needs about 6 chunks of 512 tokens for the original model.
deep:
Limitations raised at the end of the lecture and the responses:

| Limitation | Detail | Response |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Context length | 512 tokens in the original paper | local attention and similar approximations grow the context within a reasonable compute bound (Lecture 2 first half) |
| Latency and cost | BERT base has about 110 million parameters | DistilBERT: distillation with half the layers, almost the same performance |
| Training recipe | two objectives, MLM and NSP, may not both be needed | RoBERTa: drop NSP, dynamic masking, more data |

Context arithmetic: $\lceil 3000/512\rceil=6$ chunks (ignoring overlap).

Strengths to balance this: contextual embeddings, easy fine tuning for any classification task, and wide industry use for sentiment detection and other classification tasks. The remaining structural limit is that an encoder only model cannot generate text, which is why the course moves to decoder only models next.
say: BERT has three main limits. The context is 512 tokens, so long documents must be chunked, and attention tricks like local attention can extend it. The base model has about 110 million parameters, which is costly and slow for many uses, and DistilBERT addressed that with distillation. And the two pretraining objectives may not both be needed, which RoBERTa tested by dropping next sentence prediction. On top of that, it can't generate text at all. Even so, BERT style encoders are still widely used for sentiment and classification.

followups.q: How do you handle documents longer than 512 tokens with the original model?
followups.a: Chunk them, or use a variant with a longer context built with local attention tricks.

followups.q: Which fix targets latency?
followups.a: DistilBERT, which halves the layers and uses distillation to keep quality.

topic: CME295 L3: LLMs, MoE, decoding and inference
q: What is a large language model, and what makes it large?
plain: A large language model (LLM) assigns probabilities to token sequences, which lets it write text one token at a time. It is large in three ways: parameters, training data and computing power. Parameters (the numbers the model learns) usually number at least about a billion, and the biggest reach hundreds of billions. Training data is counted in tokens, from hundreds of billions up to tens of trillions. Training and running the largest models needs many graphics processing units (GPUs). An encoder only model does not count as an LLM, because it does not produce text. Almost all modern LLMs are decoder only, meaning they keep only the masked self attention and feed forward layers. For example, a model with 70 billion parameters trained on 10 trillion tokens counts as an LLM.
deep:
A language model assigns probability to sequences of tokens. Here it always predicts the probability of the next token. An LLM is a language model that is large in three senses:

- Size: at least on the order of a billion parameters, often hundreds of billions.
- Data: hundreds of billions to tens of trillions of pretraining tokens.
- Compute: many GPUs, although optimizations now let models run on consumer GPUs.

The terminology is recent. In 2018 and 2019 there was no real definition, and BERT was sometimes included. With the now established definition, a model must do text to text generation, so an encoder only model such as BERT is not an LLM.

Architecture: decoder only. Remove the encoder and cross attention and keep masked self attention, the feed forward network and add and norm. More than 90 percent of modern LLMs are decoder only, for example GPT, Llama, Gemma, DeepSeek, Mistral and Qwen.
say: A large language model is a language model, meaning it assigns probabilities to sequences of tokens, that is large in three ways: parameters, training data and compute. Think at least around a billion parameters, hundreds of billions to tens of trillions of training tokens, and many GPUs. By the current definition it has to produce text, so an encoder only model like BERT doesn't count. In practice, more than ninety percent of modern LLMs, like Llama, Gemma, DeepSeek, Mistral and Qwen, are decoder only, keeping masked self attention and feed forward layers. The terminology is recent, and in 2018 and 2019 nobody had a settled definition.
must_mention: language model: probabilities over token sequences
large in parameters, data and compute
must generate text, so BERT is not an LLM

followups.q: Why is BERT not an LLM?
followups.a: It is encoder only and produces embeddings, not text, and the current definition requires text generation.

followups.q: What does decoder only mean in practice?
followups.a: Each layer keeps masked self attention and a feed forward network, with no encoder and no cross attention.

traps: Calling any transformer an LLM. The definition needs generation and large scale.

topic: CME295 L3: LLMs, MoE, decoding and inference
q: What is a mixture of experts, and how do dense and sparse versions differ?
plain: A mixture of experts (MoE) has several expert networks, and each input uses only some of them. A small network called the gate, or router, gives each expert a weight. The output is the sum of each expert's answer multiplied by its weight. In a dense MoE, every expert is used, with weights between 0 and 1 that add up to 1. In a sparse MoE, only the top k experts are used, where k is often 1 or 2. Sparse MoE needs fewer floating point operations (FLOPs, a count of additions and multiplications), so it costs less to run. For example, with 8 experts and k of 2, each token uses a quarter of the expert compute.
deep:
Motivation: a forward pass of a model with hundreds of billions of parameters activates all of them. Mixture of experts activates only a subset. With $n$ experts $E_i$ and a gate (router) network $G$ that scores them:

$$
\hat y=\sum_{i=1}^{n}G(x)_i\,E_i(x)
$$

- Dense MoE: no constraint on how many experts are involved, so the weights lie between 0 and 1 and behave like a probability distribution, with more weight on some experts.
- Sparse MoE: keep only the top $k$ experts (often $k=1$ or 2, a hyperparameter): $\hat y=\sum_{i\in\mathrm{TopK}}G(x)_i E_i(x)$.

FLOPs (floating point operations: additions and multiplications) measure the compute of a pass, and a sparse MoE has fewer FLOPs than a dense one. Gate and experts are trained jointly: forward pass, loss, backpropagation. The challenge is keeping the experts evenly used (routing collapse).
say: A mixture of experts replaces one big layer with several expert networks plus a router, called a gate, that decides how much each expert contributes. The output is the sum of the expert outputs weighted by the gate. In a dense version every expert contributes with a weight between zero and one, which saves nothing. In a sparse version only the top k experts run, often one or two, so the compute per token drops while total parameters stay large. Everything is trained jointly with the usual loss and backpropagation. The challenge is keeping the experts evenly used.
must_mention: several experts plus a gate or router
output is the gate weighted sum of expert outputs
dense: all experts, weights in 0 to 1
sparse: only the top k experts

followups.q: How are the gate and experts trained?
followups.a: Jointly, with the normal forward pass, loss and backpropagation.

followups.q: Why does sparse MoE save compute but dense does not?
followups.a: Dense still runs every expert and only reweights them, while sparse skips the experts not selected.

traps: Saying MoE has fewer total parameters. It has more total parameters but fewer active ones.

topic: CME295 L3: LLMs, MoE, decoding and inference
q: Where is the mixture of experts placed in an LLM, and is routing per token or per sequence?
plain: MoE replaces the feed forward network in each transformer block, because that is where most of the parameters sit. A feed forward layer has about 2 times model size times hidden size weights, more than attention. Each expert is itself a feed forward network, and the router picks the top 1 or 2 of them. Routing happens per token, so different tokens in one sentence can go to different experts. Each layer has its own router and its own experts, and they are not shared across layers. The router is a linear layer that maps the token vector to one score per expert, followed by a softmax. For example, with model size 4,096 and hidden size 16,384, the feed forward layer has about 134 million weights. The attention projections have about 67 million.
deep:
Candidate places: masked self attention, feed forward network, or normalization. The feed forward network is the right one because it is the largest part. It maps the $d_{model}$ input to a $d_{ff}$ dimensional space and back, so it has about $2\,d_{model}\,d_{ff}$ weights (plus biases), with $d_{ff}$ larger than $d_{model}$. Attention projection matrices are $d_{model}\times d_k$ and smaller (the lecture gives $d_{model}$ in the hundreds to thousands and $d_{ff}$ in the thousands to tens of thousands).

Check: $2\cdot4096\cdot16384=134{,}217{,}728$ for the feed forward layer and $4\cdot4096^2=67{,}108{,}864$ for the four attention projections (queries, keys, values and output).

Design from the lecture:

- Experts are feed forward networks, and the layer is a sparse MoE with $k$ equal to 1 or 2.
- Routing is at the token level. The router receives the token's representation (already contextual after masked self attention) and chooses the experts for that token.
- One router per layer, trainable and layer specific, and experts are not shared between layers. The router is a projection from $x$ to $n$ dimensions followed by a softmax. There is one router even though attention has many heads, because the heads were concatenated and projected before the feed forward block.
- Only the selected experts' outputs are computed.
say: I put the experts in the feed forward network, because that's where most parameters live. It has about two times the model dimension times the hidden dimension in weights, and the hidden dimension is larger than the model dimension, whereas attention matrices are smaller. So each expert is a feed forward network and the router picks the top one or two. Routing is per token, so different tokens in the same sentence can use different experts. Each layer has its own router and its own experts, and the router is a linear layer followed by a softmax over the experts. Only the chosen experts actually run.
must_mention: experts replace the feed forward network
separate router and experts per layer

followups.q: Why not put experts in the attention layer?
followups.a: Its matrices are much smaller, so there is less compute to save, and the feed forward layer dominates the parameter count.

followups.q: Is there a router per attention head?
followups.a: No. One router per layer, because the heads are concatenated and projected before the feed forward block.

traps: Saying the router sees whole sequences. It routes each token separately.

topic: CME295 L3: LLMs, MoE, decoding and inference
q: What is routing collapse in a mixture of experts, and how does the load balancing loss prevent it?
plain: Routing collapse is when the router keeps sending tokens to the same one or two experts while the others sit unused. The unused experts never learn, so the model wastes its extra capacity. The fix is an extra loss term that pushes the routing toward an even spread. For each expert it multiplies the share of tokens sent there by the router's average probability for it. These products are added up and scaled by the number of experts and a small weight called alpha. The total is smallest when every expert gets the same share. With 4 experts, a perfectly even split gives 1.0, and sending everything to one expert gives 4.0. Another trick, noisy gating, adds random noise to the router scores so other experts sometimes get picked.
deep:
Problem: during training the router can end up always choosing the same experts, so the others are never activated and never trained. This is routing collapse.

Mitigation (the auxiliary loss added to the main loss):

$$
\mathcal{L}_{aux}=\alpha\,n\sum_{i=1}^{n}f_i\,P_i
$$

with $n$ experts, hyperparameter $\alpha$, $f_i$ the fraction of tokens routed to expert $i$, and $P_i$ the average routing probability for expert $i$ (the mean of the gate's softmax output $i$ over tokens). The lecture's point is that this extra loss makes both quantities converge toward uniform distributions, which mitigates collapse.

Numbers ($n=4$, ignoring $\alpha$): uniform $f=P=(0.25,\dots)$ gives $n\sum f_iP_i=1.0$, the minimum. Total collapse $f=P=(1,0,0,0)$ gives 4.0. A mild imbalance $f=P=(0.4,0.3,0.2,0.1)$ gives 1.2.

Differentiability (Q and A): $P_i$ is a clean function of the gate output, while $f_i$ is a count of routed tokens, which the lecturer did not detail. Libraries implement it, and the lecture suggests the reasoning is not essential.

Other tools: noisy gating (add noise to the gate outputs so other experts are chosen by chance, a dropout like idea) and dropout itself can be combined with it. The quantities are computed per mini batch during regular training.
say: Routing collapse is when the router sends almost every token to the same one or two experts, so the rest never train and the capacity is wasted. The standard fix is an auxiliary loss, alpha times the number of experts times the sum over experts of f i times P i, where f i is the fraction of tokens routed to expert i and P i is the average router probability for it. That sum is minimized when both are uniform. With four experts a perfectly even split gives one and total collapse gives four. Noisy gating, which adds random noise to the router scores, is another trick that gives other experts a chance.
must_mention: router keeps picking the same experts
auxiliary loss alpha n sum f i P i
f i is the token fraction, P i the average probability

followups.q: Which of f i and P i carries the gradient?
followups.a: P i, the average gate probability, is a smooth function of the router. The routed fraction f i is a count that does not carry gradient by itself.

followups.q: What is the value of the balance term for a perfectly even split with n experts?
followups.a: 1, because n times n terms of one over n squared equals 1.

topic: CME295 L3: LLMs, MoE, decoding and inference
q: Why do mixture of experts models have more parameters but not more compute per token?
plain: A mixture of experts adds many experts, so the total number of parameters grows a lot. But each token uses only a few, so the active parameters (those used in one pass) stay small. That is how models reach the trillion parameter scale without a matching rise in compute. The Switch Transformer paper scaled past a trillion parameters and was also more sample efficient. Sample efficient means reaching a given quality with less training time. The cost is memory, because all experts must still be stored, and extra work to keep the load balanced. For example, 8 experts of 5 billion each, with 2 used per token, store 40 billion but use 10 billion.
deep:
Increasing the number of experts increases the total number of parameters (the model's capacity) but not the number of active parameters, the ones used in one forward pass. So you can scale the model without paying much more compute at inference. That is why MoE based models can exceed the hundreds of billions of parameters of dense models and reach the order of trillions (the lecture recommends the Switch Transformer paper, scaled to over a trillion parameters).

The paper also shows these models are more sample efficient: plotted against training time, they reach a given quality sooner than a dense model with fewer parameters. The lecture's summary is that everything here is a trade off.

Arithmetic: 8 experts with 5 billion parameters each give 40 billion stored expert parameters. With $k=2$, 10 billion are active per token, so the active share is $k/n=25$ percent.

Costs (standard background): every expert must sit in memory even if few are used, routing needs load balancing, and communication between devices grows when experts live on different machines.
say: A mixture of experts decouples total parameters from active parameters. Adding experts increases the total, which raises the model's capacity, but each token only uses the top few, so compute per token stays roughly flat. That's how models reach a trillion parameters. For example, eight experts of five billion parameters with two used per token store forty billion but use ten billion. The Switch Transformer paper also reported better sample efficiency, meaning less training time for the same quality. The cost is memory, since every expert must be stored, and the engineering needed to keep the load balanced across experts.
must_mention: capacity grows, compute per token stays flat

followups.q: What are active parameters?
followups.a: The parameters actually used in one forward pass, so only the selected experts plus the shared layers.

followups.q: What does sample efficient mean?
followups.a: Reaching a given quality with less training time or data.

traps: Saying MoE is cheaper in memory. All experts must be stored.

topic: CME295 L3: LLMs, MoE, decoding and inference
q: Why is greedy decoding not enough, and how does beam search improve on it?
plain: Greedy decoding picks the single most likely token at every step. It gives the same output every time, and it can miss the best whole sequence. Beam search keeps the k most likely partial sequences at each step, and k is called the beam size. At the end it returns the complete sequence with the highest total probability. Suppose A has 0.6 and B has 0.4 at step one. The best next token then has 0.4 after A but 0.9 after B. Greedy follows A for 0.24, while beam search with k of 2 finds B for 0.36.
deep:
The model outputs a distribution over the next token, and we need a rule to choose.

Greedy decoding: take the arg max token each step. It is the first natural idea but has two problems. It is deterministic, so a given input always gives the same output, with no diversity. And it is locally optimal but not globally optimal: the goal is a high probability sequence $\prod_t p(y_t\mid y_{<t})$, which repeated local maxima do not guarantee.

Beam search keeps track of the $k$ most probable paths ($k$ is the beam size or beam width). Start with BOS. At each step, expand each kept path with every next token, and keep the best $k$ paths overall. At the end, pick the highest scoring complete sequence.

Example: step one A 0.6, B 0.4. After A the best continuation is 0.4, after B it is 0.9. Greedy: $0.6\times0.4=0.24$. Beam search with $k=2$ keeps both A and B, then finds $0.4\times0.9=0.36$.

Costs: bookkeeping and extra computation, and the result is the most likely sequence, which is less diverse and less creative.
say: Greedy decoding takes the most likely token at every step. It's deterministic, so there's no variety, and it's only locally optimal: a strong first token can lead to weak later ones. Beam search fixes part of that by keeping the k most probable partial sequences, called the beam, and expanding each one at every step, then returning the sequence with the highest total probability. For example, if A has 0.6 and B has 0.4, but the best continuation after A is 0.4 and after B is 0.9, greedy gets 0.24 while beam search finds 0.36. The cost is more computation and less diversity.
must_mention: greedy picks the arg max each step
beam search keeps k best paths
picks the highest total probability sequence

followups.q: Is beam search guaranteed to find the best sequence?
followups.a: No. It is only closer to global optimality than greedy, and the result depends on k.

followups.q: What is the beam width?
followups.a: The number of partial sequences kept at each step, called k.

traps: Saying greedy decoding is random. It is fully deterministic.

topic: CME295 L3: LLMs, MoE, decoding and inference
q: How is a beam search candidate scored, why does it favor short sequences, and when is beam search used?
plain: Beam search scores a sequence by adding up the logarithms of its token probabilities. The logarithm turns a long product of small numbers into a sum, which is easier to handle. Each probability is below 1, so every extra token lowers the total score. That makes plain beam search prefer shorter sequences. The fix is a length penalty, such as dividing the score by the number of tokens raised to a small power. Beam search is slower and less creative than sampling, so chat models rarely use it. It is still common in machine translation, where the most likely output is what you want. For example, 5 tokens at probability 0.5 each give 0.031, and 10 tokens give 0.001.
deep:
Score of a sequence: $\log P(y)=\sum_{t=1}^{N}\log p(y_t\mid y_{<t})$, the log of the product of next token probabilities (the lecture writes it as the log probability of A given BOS, plus cute given BOS and A, and so on).

Since every factor is between 0 and 1, the product shrinks as tokens are added, so unnormalized beam search prioritizes shorter sequences. A length term counteracts it, on the order of one over the number of tokens to some power:

$$
\mathrm{score}(y)=\frac{1}{N^{\alpha}}\sum_{t=1}^{N}\log p(y_t\mid y_{<t})
$$

Numbers: $0.5^5=0.03125$ against $0.5^{10}=0.00098$.

Practical notes from the lecture: tracking the most probable paths and saving them requires a lot of computation, and the output is what the model finds very likely, whereas often you want it more diverse or creative. So beam search is not what people typically use for chat. It is used for tasks like machine translation, where something close to the most likely output is the aim. Most systems sample instead.
say: Beam search scores a candidate sequence by the sum of the log probabilities of its tokens, which is the log of the product. Since every probability is below one, each extra token lowers the score, so plain beam search favors short sequences. The fix is a length normalization, such as dividing by the number of tokens to some power. It also needs more compute and memory to track k paths, and it produces likely but bland output, so chat models rarely use it. It's still common in machine translation, where I want the most likely output rather than a creative one.
must_mention: score is the sum of log probabilities
probabilities below one shrink the product

followups.q: Why use logs?
followups.a: They turn a product of many small probabilities into a sum, which is stable and easy to compare.

followups.q: What does the length penalty look like?
followups.a: Divide the log probability sum by the number of tokens raised to a power alpha, so longer sequences are not punished just for being long.

traps: Forgetting the length bias and concluding beam search always yields the best sequence.

topic: CME295 L3: LLMs, MoE, decoding and inference
q: How do sampling, top k and top p decoding work?
plain: Sampling draws the next token at random, using the model's probabilities as the odds. Likely tokens are drawn often and unlikely ones rarely, so answers vary between runs. Restricting the choice avoids drawing very unlikely tokens. Top k sampling keeps only the k most likely tokens and samples among them. Top p sampling keeps the smallest group of top tokens whose probabilities add up to at least p. For example, take probabilities 0.5, 0.3, 0.1, 0.05 and 0.05. Top k of 2 keeps the first two, rescaled to 0.625 and 0.375. Top p of 0.9 keeps the first three.
deep:
Sampling uses the distribution itself to pick the next token, so more probable tokens are drawn more often. It gives the diversity and creativity that greedy and beam search lack, and it is the third and typical method in chat systems. Nothing else in the transformer is random.

Because very low probability tokens can still be drawn, we restrict the candidates:

- Top k: keep the $k$ most probable tokens (for $k=4$, the four best) and sample among them.
- Top p (nucleus): keep the smallest set $S_p$ of most probable tokens with $\sum_{i\in S_p}p_i\ge p$. The set size adapts to how peaked the distribution is.

After either filter, rescale the kept probabilities to sum to 1. Check with $(0.5,0.3,0.1,0.05,0.05)$: cumulative sums are $0.5,0.8,0.9,0.95,1.0$, so $p=0.9$ keeps three tokens, and $k=2$ keeps two, rescaled to $0.625$ and $0.375$.

Greedy decoding is the case $k=1$. Sampling is for inference only: training compares the output probabilities with the (usually hard) label.
say: With sampling, I draw the next token from the model's probability distribution, so likely tokens come up often and the output varies between runs. To avoid drawing very unlikely tokens I restrict the choice. Top k keeps the k most likely tokens and samples among them. Top p, also called nucleus sampling, keeps the smallest set of top tokens whose probabilities add up to at least p, so the set size adapts to the shape of the distribution. After either, I rescale the kept probabilities to sum to one. With probabilities 0.5, 0.3, 0.1 and two small ones, top k of two keeps two tokens, and top p of 0.9 keeps three.
must_mention: top k: fixed number of candidates
top p: smallest set with cumulative probability at least p

followups.q: What is the difference between top k and top p?
followups.a: Top k keeps a fixed number of tokens, while top p keeps a variable number that depends on how concentrated the distribution is.

followups.q: What is greedy decoding in these terms?
followups.a: Top k with k equal to 1.

traps: Saying top p keeps tokens with probability above p. It keeps tokens until the cumulative probability reaches p.

topic: CME295 L3: LLMs, MoE, decoding and inference
q: What does temperature do to the next token distribution, and how would you set it?
plain: Temperature controls how spiky or flat the next token probabilities are. Before the softmax (the step that turns scores into probabilities), every score is divided by the temperature T. A low temperature makes the top token even more likely, so output is focused and repeatable. A high temperature flattens the odds, so unlikely tokens get drawn more and output is more creative. Use low values for facts, code and extraction, and higher values for creative writing. For example, scores 2.0, 1.0 and 0.1 give 0.66, 0.24 and 0.10 at T of 1. At T of 0.5 they sharpen to 0.86, 0.12 and 0.02. At T of 2 they flatten to 0.50, 0.30 and 0.19.
deep:
The final layers of the transformer project the $d_{model}$ vector to the vocabulary size $V$ (a linear layer) and apply a softmax with temperature $T$:

$$
p_i=\frac{e^{z_i/T}}{\sum_{j=1}^{V}e^{z_j/T}}
$$

$T=1$ is the plain softmax. $T<1$ sharpens (spiky distribution), $T>1$ flattens (closer to uniform). In the limits, $T\to0$ is greedy and $T\to\infty$ is uniform over the vocabulary.

Worked values for logits $(2.0,1.0,0.1)$:

| T | probabilities |
| --- | --- |
| 0.1 | 1.00, 0.00, 0.00 |
| 0.5 | 0.86, 0.12, 0.02 |
| 1 | 0.66, 0.24, 0.10 |
| 2 | 0.50, 0.30, 0.19 |
| 10 | 0.37, 0.33, 0.30 |

Choosing: for something creative use a higher temperature, and for more deterministic, high quality, reliable output use a lower one. With any strictly positive temperature, repeated runs on the same input give different outputs. Nothing in the transformer itself is random: only the sampling step is.
say: Temperature divides the logits by T before the softmax. A low temperature makes the distribution spikier, so the top token dominates and output is focused and repeatable. A high temperature flattens it, so unlikely tokens get sampled more and output is more creative. For example, logits two, one and 0.1 give about 0.66, 0.24 and 0.10 at temperature one, 0.86, 0.12 and 0.02 at 0.5, and 0.50, 0.30 and 0.19 at two. So I use low values for facts, code and extraction, and higher ones for creative writing. At the limit, zero is greedy decoding and infinity is a uniform draw over the vocabulary.
must_mention: divide logits by T inside the softmax
low T spiky, high T flat
T near 0 is greedy, large T is uniform
low for reliable output, high for creative

followups.q: Does temperature change which token is most likely?
followups.a: No. The ranking stays the same, only the gaps between probabilities change.

followups.q: What temperature gives greedy decoding?
followups.a: T going to 0, so the top token gets probability 1.

traps: Thinking temperature changes the model weights. It only rescales the logits at sampling time.

topic: CME295 L3: LLMs, MoE, decoding and inference
q: Prove that as the temperature goes to zero the softmax becomes one hot, and as it goes to infinity it becomes uniform.
plain: Factor out the largest score from every term, so the biggest term becomes exactly 1. Every other term becomes e to the power of minus a positive gap over T. As T shrinks toward 0, the gap over T grows without limit, so those terms go to 0. Then the top token gets probability 1 and the rest get 0. As T grows without limit, every gap over T goes to 0, and each term goes to 1. Then every token gets probability 1 over the vocabulary size. For example, with 3 tokens and T huge, each gets about 0.333. So low T acts like greedy decoding and high T acts like uniform random choice.
deep:
Let $k=\arg\max_j z_j$ (assume it is unique). Multiply numerator and denominator by $e^{-z_k/T}$:

$$
p_i=\frac{e^{z_i/T}}{\sum_j e^{z_j/T}}=\frac{e^{(z_i-z_k)/T}}{\sum_j e^{(z_j-z_k)/T}}
$$

The gaps $z_j-z_k\le0$, and the term $j=k$ is exactly $e^0=1$ whatever $T$ is.

- $T\to0^+$: for $j\ne k$, $(z_j-z_k)/T\to-\infty$, so $e^{(z_j-z_k)/T}\to0$. The denominator tends to $1$, so $p_k\to1$ and $p_i=\frac{e^{(z_i-z_k)/T}}{1}\to0$ for $i\ne k$. This is one hot on the largest logit.
- $T\to\infty$: every exponent $(z_j-z_k)/T\to0$, every term tends to $e^0=1$, and $p_i\to1/V$. This is the uniform distribution.

If several logits tie for the maximum, the mass splits equally among them. Numerical check for logits $(2,1,0.1)$: $T=0.1$ gives $(1.000,0.000,0.000)$ and $T=10$ gives $(0.366,0.331,0.303)$.

Q and A in the lecture: asked whether the spiky case can be read as a Gaussian, the answer is that tokens are discrete and unordered, so no. Read small $T$ as a few top tokens dominating, and large $T$ as even tokens that were not the most likely getting a higher adjusted probability.
say: Let k be the index of the largest logit. I multiply the numerator and denominator of the softmax by e to the minus z k over T, so each term becomes e to the power of z j minus z k, over T. The gap z j minus z k is zero for the top token and negative for all others. As T goes to zero, the negative gaps divided by T go to minus infinity, so those terms vanish, the denominator tends to one, and the top token gets probability one. As T goes to infinity, every exponent goes to zero, each term goes to one, and every token gets one over the vocabulary size.
must_mention: factor out the exponential of the largest logit over T
gaps are zero for the top token, negative otherwise
T to infinity: uniform over the vocabulary

followups.q: What happens with tied top logits as T goes to 0?
followups.a: The probability mass splits equally among the tied tokens.

followups.q: Why is a Gaussian a poor picture of a spiky distribution here?
followups.a: Tokens are discrete and have no natural order, so there is no continuous axis to put a bell curve on.

topic: CME295 L3: LLMs, MoE, decoding and inference
q: Is the transformer deterministic, and why can temperature zero still give different outputs?
plain: The transformer's math is deterministic: the same input always gives the same probabilities. The only random step is sampling the next token from those probabilities. With temperature 0 you always take the top token, so in theory the output never changes. In practice it can still change, because of how graphics processing units (GPUs) add numbers. Adding the same numbers in a different order can give slightly different results, because computers round after each step. The order of additions can change with batch size and server load. Those tiny differences can flip which token is on top when two tokens are almost tied. For example, two tokens at 0.400001 and 0.400000 can swap places after tiny rounding differences.
deep:
In theory: all computation in the transformer is deterministic and the only non deterministic piece is sampling the next token. With $T=0$ you always take the arg max, so the output is one fixed thing.

In practice, $T=0$ can still give different outputs. Floating point addition is not associative, so $(a+b)+c\ne a+(b+c)$ in general. When GPUs reduce (sum) many numbers on very different scales, the order of the operations matters, and that order can depend on the kernel, the batch size, how requests are batched together and server load. The tiny numerical differences can flip the arg max where two tokens are nearly tied. After one different token the whole continuation diverges.

The lecture calls this beyond the scope of the class and recommends an optional recent article on defeating non determinism in LLM inference, whose high level idea is the one above. A practical consequence: do not assume exact reproducibility from $T=0$ in a hosted API, and design tests that tolerate variation.
say: The transformer itself is deterministic: the same input gives the same probabilities. The only random step is sampling from them. So with temperature zero, in theory, the output never changes. In practice it can, because floating point addition isn't associative, and GPUs sum numbers in an order that can vary with batch size, kernels and server load. Those tiny rounding differences can flip the top token when two are nearly tied, and then the text diverges from there. There's a recent write up on defeating nondeterminism in LLM inference that explains it, which I'd cite if asked.
must_mention: floating point addition is not associative
near ties flip and text diverges

followups.q: How would you test an LLM feature given this?
followups.a: Allow tolerance, compare meaning or constraints rather than exact strings, and fix settings, but do not rely on perfect reproducibility.

followups.q: Does a seed fix it?
followups.a: A seed fixes sampling randomness, but numeric nondeterminism from kernels can remain.

traps: Saying temperature 0 guarantees identical outputs across runs.

topic: CME295 L3: LLMs, MoE, decoding and inference
q: What is guided decoding, and why is it better than asking the model again until the output is valid?
plain: Guided decoding forces output into a set format, such as JSON (a text format for data), by blocking invalid tokens. The naive way is to ask for JSON, check the result, and ask again if it is wrong. That wastes time and can fail many times. With guided decoding, at each step only tokens allowed by the format keep a nonzero probability. For example, out of 50,000 tokens, a JSON object can start with only a handful, such as an opening bracket. If several tokens are allowed, the model picks among them with its usual method. The allowed set is tracked with tools such as finite state machines (step by step rule checkers) or grammars.
deep:
Naive approach: ask for the format, validate the output, and repeat until it is valid. This costs repeated generations and has no guarantee.

Guided (constrained) decoding: during generation, filter out the invalid next tokens. At each step compute the set of tokens that keep the output valid for the target format, give all others zero probability (set their logits to $-\infty$ before the softmax), and sample or pick among the remainder with the usual strategy. For JSON the first token must open the brace, then comes a property name, and so on. Sometimes more than one token is allowed, and then the normal next token strategy chooses.

How the allowed set is computed: the lecture points to finite state machines (FSM) and context free grammars and does not go into details. It guarantees syntactic validity of the format, not the correctness of the content.
say: Guided decoding forces the output to follow a format, like valid JSON, by filtering the next token at every step. The naive alternative is to ask the model for JSON, validate, and retry if it fails, which wastes time and can fail repeatedly. With guided decoding, I track the state of the format with a finite state machine or a grammar, and any token that would break it gets zero probability. For example, a JSON object must start with an opening brace, so that's the only allowed first token. If several tokens are allowed, I sample among them as usual. It guarantees syntax, not correctness of the content.
must_mention: filter invalid next tokens each step
finite state machine or grammar tracks validity

followups.q: How are invalid tokens blocked?
followups.a: Their logits are set to minus infinity, or their probability is zeroed, before sampling.

followups.q: What does it not guarantee?
followups.a: Semantic correctness. A valid JSON object can still hold wrong values.

topic: CME295 L3: LLMs, MoE, decoding and inference
q: What is context length, and what is context rot?
plain: Context length, also called context size or window, is how many tokens a model can take in at once. Modern models range from tens of thousands to millions of tokens. A longer context does not guarantee better answers. Context rot is the drop in the model's ability to use information as the context grows. Needle in a haystack tests hide one fact in a long text and ask the model to find it. Accuracy falls as the text grows, and distractors (irrelevant but similar text) make it fall faster. So put only the most relevant context in front of the model. For example, a model with a 1,000,000 token window may find a fact better in 5,000 tokens than in 500,000.
deep:
Context length (also called context size or window size) is the length of the input measured in tokens. It is what is exposed to self attention, and the complexity tricks from lecture 2 (sparse attention and similar) keep the cost from growing like $n^2$. Orders of magnitude: tens of thousands, hundreds of thousands or millions of tokens, for example some Gemini models in the million range.

More context does not solve everything. Context rot (named in a paper from the summer of 2025) tests the ability to retrieve a piece of information in a needle in a haystack setup: bury the answer in longer and longer text and measure whether the model surfaces it. Retrieval ability decreases as the context length grows. The paper also controls for what else is in the context: distractors (noise) reduce retrieval further, so what is in your context matters, not just its length.

Implication: when you use an LLM to solve a retrieval problem, target as much as possible the right piece of context for the model to see and predict on, which motivates retrieval augmented generation (Lecture 7).
say: Context length, also called context size or window, is how many tokens the model can take in one pass. Modern models go from tens of thousands to millions of tokens. But more context doesn't automatically mean better answers. Context rot is the drop in the model's ability to use information as the context grows, shown by needle in a haystack tests, where one fact is buried in a long text. Distractors make it worse. So for retrieval problems, I'd try to give the model just the right piece of context rather than everything, which is the idea behind retrieval augmented generation.
must_mention: context length is measured in tokens
context rot: retrieval degrades with length

followups.q: How would you design around context rot?
followups.a: Retrieve and include only the most relevant passages, keep irrelevant text out, and test retrieval on your own long inputs.

followups.q: Is context length the same as the attention span?
followups.a: Yes, it is what self attention covers, with tricks keeping the cost below n squared.

traps: Assuming a million token window means the model uses all of it equally well.

topic: CME295 L3: LLMs, MoE, decoding and inference
q: What are zero shot and few shot prompting, and what are the usual parts of a prompt?
plain: A prompt usually has four parts: context, instructions, inputs and constraints. Context sets the scene, instructions say the task, inputs give the data, and constraints limit the answer. Zero shot prompting gives only the task, with no examples. Few shot prompting adds a few input and output examples before the real question. Both are in context learning, where the model learns the task from the prompt without any weight change. Examples usually steer the model well, but they cost tokens and effort to collect. With strong newer models, clear instructions can match few shot, since examples can narrow how the model generalizes. For example, 3 story examples at 200 tokens each add 600 tokens to every request.
deep:
Prompt structure (no formal theory, but a useful mental model): context (set the setting and the kind of query), instructions (the task), inputs (what the task operates on) and constraints (limits on the response). In a chat product the context may be a line such as the model name and the date, the instructions are the user's query plus its inputs, and constraints such as safety rules are present in the prompt but hidden from the user.

In context learning puts the task in the prompt:

- Zero shot: only the input query.
- Few shot: examples of inputs and outputs first (the lecture's example: stories for teddy bears named Teddy, then Bob).

Trade offs: examples steer the model toward the target task, and it connects the dots from what it learned in training. But gathering them is costly and they add tokens to the context window, so more compute. With newer models that have reasoning capabilities, few shot is generally better but not always: better instructions can make zero shot on par or better, because examples constrain the model to a finite set that may not match the data distribution at inference time. Explaining the task in natural language lets the model use its reasoning ability, as in the Plan and Solve paper, where the model plans and then solves.
say: A prompt typically has context, instructions, inputs and constraints. Zero shot gives only the task. Few shot adds a handful of input and output examples first. Both are in context learning, since the model picks up the task from the prompt without any weight update. Examples usually steer the model well, but they cost tokens, compute and effort to collect, and they can narrow how the model generalizes. With stronger recent models, clear and reasoned instructions can match or beat few shot examples, so it's worth trying both. For instance, three examples of two hundred tokens each add six hundred tokens to every request.
must_mention: examples cost tokens and can constrain
good instructions can match few shot

followups.q: Does in context learning update weights?
followups.a: No. The model adapts from the prompt alone.

followups.q: When would you prefer instructions over examples?
followups.a: When examples are costly or too narrow for the real distribution, and the model is strong at following reasoned instructions.

traps: Saying few shot is always better. Newer models often do as well with clear instructions.

topic: CME295 L3: LLMs, MoE, decoding and inference
q: What is chain of thought prompting, and what are its benefits and costs?
plain: Chain of thought makes the model write its reasoning steps before the final answer. Writing the steps first tends to give more accurate answers, especially for math and logic. It also helps debugging, because you can read the steps and see where the reasoning went wrong. If the steps assume the year is 2019, you can spot a wrong date in the prompt. The cost is more output tokens, so answers take longer and cost more. You can trigger it with few shot examples that include reasoning, or with an instruction to think step by step. For example, if reasoning adds 300 tokens to a 20 token answer, the output is 16 times longer.
deep:
Idea: force the model to produce a rationale before the answer. Researchers saw higher performance, because the answer follows from explicit intermediate steps. The lecture's example: asked how old the teddy bear is, a direct numeric answer cannot show why, while the full chain makes clear what led to the answer. It composes with in context learning: few shot examples can include the reasoning and the answer, and the model adjusts reasoning and response to a changed query.

Debugging: you do not look at weights as in the old days. The reasoning is interpretable in tokens, so you can root cause a failure, for instance seeing in the chain that the model assumed the wrong year because of a date in your context.

Cost: it increases the number of tokens, so inference takes longer, which is usually acceptable. Arithmetic: $(300+20)/20=16$. The zero shot trigger phrase (think step by step) is standard background.
say: Chain of thought makes the model write its reasoning before the final answer. That tends to improve accuracy on math and logic, because the answer follows from explicit steps. It also helps debugging: instead of inspecting weights, I read the steps and see where it went wrong, like spotting a wrong date in the prompt. I can trigger it with few shot examples that include reasoning or with an instruction to think step by step. The cost is more output tokens, so higher latency and cost. For example, three hundred reasoning tokens on a twenty token answer makes the output sixteen times longer.
must_mention: few shot reasoning examples or think step by step

followups.q: Why does writing the steps help?
followups.a: The model computes the answer through intermediate tokens instead of jumping straight to a number, which gives it more computation and a visible trace.

followups.q: What is the main downside?
followups.a: More generated tokens, so higher latency and cost.

traps: Treating the written reasoning as a guaranteed faithful explanation of the model's internals.

topic: CME295 L3: LLMs, MoE, decoding and inference
q: What is self consistency, and how does it improve chain of thought?
plain: Self consistency samples several reasoning paths for the same question and picks the answer that appears most often. Each path is drawn with some randomness, so the paths differ. You then pull out the final answer from each path and take a majority vote. Errors tend to scatter across different wrong answers, while right reasoning tends to agree. The samples run in parallel, so the delay is about that of the slowest one, but the cost is higher. To extract answers, ask the model to put the answer last, then use a pattern match or another model. For example, if 5 samples give 18, 18, 17, 18 and 20, the vote picks 18 with 3 of 5. You need a benchmark with known answers to check that it helps.
deep:
Procedure: sample the model several times (temperature above 0) with chain of thought, factor out the reasoning to isolate each final answer, then majority vote:

$$
\hat a=\arg\max_a\sum_{i=1}^{m}\mathbf{1}[a_i=a]
$$

It makes chain of thought stronger and more robust to individual reasoning errors. Samples are drawn in parallel from the same prompt and do not enter each other's context, so latency is roughly the maximum latency of one generation, while token cost is multiplied by $m$.

Answer extraction: add an instruction to put the actual answer last and take the last item, use a regex, or use another LLM to extract it. Evaluation: you need a benchmark with ground truth labels to assert it is better. The original paper used arithmetic and math benchmarks.

Check: answers $(18,18,17,18,20)$ give counts $18:3$, so the vote returns 18.
say: Self consistency strengthens chain of thought by sampling several reasoning paths for the same question, at a temperature above zero, extracting the final answer from each, and taking a majority vote. Wrong reasoning tends to scatter over different answers, while correct reasoning tends to agree. The samples run in parallel, so latency is about that of the slowest one, but token cost multiplies. I'd ask the model to put the final answer last so I can extract it with a regex, or use another model to extract it. And I need a benchmark with ground truth to know it helps. For example, answers eighteen, eighteen, seventeen, eighteen and twenty vote for eighteen.
must_mention: sample several chain of thought paths
extract the final answer from each
needs a benchmark to verify the gain

followups.q: What does it do to latency and cost?
followups.a: Latency stays close to one generation if you run samples in parallel, but token cost multiplies by the number of samples.

followups.q: Why does voting help?
followups.a: Different wrong paths usually end in different wrong answers, while correct reasoning converges on the same answer.

traps: Running the samples at temperature 0, which would give identical paths.

topic: CME295 L3: LLMs, MoE, decoding and inference
q: What is the KV cache, and why does it speed up text generation?
plain: The key value (KV) cache stores the keys and values of earlier tokens so they are computed only once. When the model writes a new token, that token's query must look at the keys and values of all earlier tokens. Those earlier keys and values do not change, so recomputing them every step would be wasted work. The queries of earlier tokens are never needed again, so only keys and values are cached. Each step then computes keys and values for just the one new token. During training there is no cache, because the whole text goes through at once. The price is memory, which grows with the length of the text. For example, to write token 1,000, the cache avoids recomputing keys and values for the 999 earlier tokens.
deep:
In masked self attention each new token's query attends to the keys and values of all previous tokens. Without a cache you would recompute the key and value representations of every earlier token at each step. The KV cache stores the key and value matrices of earlier tokens (per layer) and reuses them: at each step compute $q,k,v$ for the new token only, append $k,v$ to the cache, and attend over the cached keys and values. Queries of previous tokens are not of interest for the present token, so they are not stored.

Training: teacher forcing passes all positions through at once, so the cache does not come up.

Memory per sequence: $2\cdot L\cdot n\cdot H_{kv}\cdot d_h\cdot b$ bytes, which grows linearly with the sequence length, the number of layers and the number of key value heads (4 GiB for $L=32$, $n=8192$, $H_{kv}=32$, $d_h=128$, 16 bit numbers). Everything that follows in the lecture attacks this cost: grouped query attention (fewer key value heads), PagedAttention (smarter memory layout) and multi head latent attention (compressed entries).
say: The KV cache stores the keys and values of all earlier tokens so I compute them only once. When generating a new token, its query attends to the keys and values of every earlier token, and those don't change, so recomputing them every step would be wasted. I only compute the key and value for the new token and append them. I don't cache queries, since earlier queries are never needed again. It isn't used in training, because teacher forcing processes the whole sequence at once. The price is memory that grows with sequence length, layers and the number of key value heads.
must_mention: cache keys and values of earlier tokens
compute k and v only for the new token
queries of earlier tokens are not needed
memory grows with length, layers and heads

followups.q: Why not cache queries too?
followups.a: Earlier tokens' queries are never used again, since only the current token's query attends to the past.

followups.q: What dominates the cache size?
followups.a: Sequence length times layers times key value heads times head size times bytes, times two for keys and values.

traps: Saying the KV cache is used in training. Teacher forcing computes all positions at once.

topic: CME295 L3: LLMs, MoE, decoding and inference
q: What problem does PagedAttention solve?
plain: PagedAttention stores the key value (KV) cache in small blocks instead of one big reserved chunk per request. A naive server reserves room for the longest possible text, because it does not know when the reply will end. Most of that room goes unused, which is called internal fragmentation (reserved but empty space). Gaps between blocks are called external fragmentation, and they waste space too. Reserved but unused space blocks other requests from being served. PagedAttention hands out fixed size blocks as the text grows and keeps a table that maps token positions to blocks. It powers the vLLM inference package and cuts fragmentation a lot. For example, using 300 of 2,048 reserved slots wastes 85 percent, while blocks of 16 waste only 4 slots.
deep:
Setting: an inference server handles many requests and keeps a KV cache per request. The naive layout reserves a contiguous block of the maximum context length for each request at the start, because the reply stops only at EOS and nobody knows when.

The PagedAttention paper names the waste:

- Internal fragmentation: reserved space that is never filled with real tokens.
- External fragmentation: gaps left by the memory allocator, which does not place blocks one right after another.
- Reserved but unused space also limits how many requests fit at once.

PagedAttention (the engine behind vLLM) generates in fixed size blocks (16 tokens in the paper) allocated as needed, with a mapping from token position indices to cache blocks, like pages in virtual memory. It reduces fragmentation by a lot, so the server can hold more concurrent requests.

Arithmetic: a request using 300 tokens in a 2,048 slot reservation wastes $1-300/2048=85.4$ percent. With blocks of 16 it uses $\lceil300/16\rceil=19$ blocks, which is 304 slots, so only 4 slots (1.3 percent) are empty.
say: PagedAttention manages the KV cache like virtual memory pages. A naive server reserves room for the maximum context length for every request, because it doesn't know when the reply will end, so most of that reserved space is empty, which is internal fragmentation. Gaps between blocks add external fragmentation. PagedAttention instead allocates small fixed size blocks as the text grows, with the paper using blocks of sixteen tokens, and keeps a table mapping token positions to blocks. That lets the server hold many more concurrent requests. It's the idea behind the vLLM serving library. For example, three hundred tokens in a two thousand slot reservation wastes eighty five percent, while blocks waste only a handful of slots.
must_mention: naive reservation of maximum context per request
fixed size blocks with a position to block table

followups.q: Why not just reserve less memory?
followups.a: The reply length is unknown, and if a request exceeds its reservation it fails, so servers over reserve unless they allocate on demand in blocks.

followups.q: What is the analogy?
followups.a: Virtual memory paging: logical token positions map to physical blocks that need not be contiguous.

topic: CME295 L3: LLMs, MoE, decoding and inference
q: What is multi head latent attention (MLA), and how does it shrink the KV cache?
plain: Multi head latent attention (MLA), from DeepSeek, stores one small compressed vector per token instead of full keys and values. It first projects the token vector down to a smaller latent space (a compressed space). Keys and values are then rebuilt from that latent vector by separate expansion matrices. The same compressed vector serves keys, values and all heads, so the cache holds one per token and layer. The expansion matrices stay separate, so keys and values can still differ. The DeepSeek V2 paper also reported better quality, possibly a regularization effect. For example, 8,192 cached numbers per token shrink to a 512 number latent, which is 16 times smaller.
deep:
Vanilla multi head attention: a token representation $h$ is projected by $H$ key matrices and $H$ value matrices, so per token and layer you cache $2Hd_h$ numbers, and these vectors are long.

MLA factorizes each projection through a lower dimensional latent space: a down projection compresses, and up projections decompress:

$$
c=W^{DKV}h,\qquad k_i=W_i^{UK}c,\qquad v_i=W_i^{UV}c
$$

The key simplifications described in the lecture: the compression matrix is shared across keys and values, and shared across the $H$ heads, so you cache only $c$, one vector per token and per transformer block. The decompression matrices stay separate to learn different keys and values. The latent dimension is a fixed design choice, the same for everyone (it could differ, but in practice it is the same). The DeepSeek V2 paper also reports a performance improvement, credited to a regularization effect from sharing, so the benefit is not only hardware related.

Illustration with an assumed configuration: $2\cdot32\cdot128=8192$ cached numbers per token and layer for full multi head attention against a 512 dimensional latent gives a $16\times$ reduction. (DeepSeek V2 also keeps a small extra positional key for rotary embeddings, standard background not covered in the lecture.)
say: Multi head latent attention, from DeepSeek, shrinks the KV cache by compressing keys and values into a small latent vector. I project the token representation down to a low dimensional latent, cache just that, and rebuild the keys and values with separate up projection matrices when needed. The compression is shared across keys and values and across all heads, so each token and layer stores one small vector instead of two full sets of per head vectors. The up projections stay separate so keys and values can still differ. DeepSeek V2 also reported better quality, possibly from a regularizing effect. For example, shrinking eight thousand numbers to five hundred twelve is sixteen times smaller.
must_mention: down project to a low dimensional latent
rebuild keys and values with up projections
shared across keys, values and heads
fixed latent size, possible quality gain

followups.q: How does MLA differ from GQA?
followups.a: GQA shares whole key and value heads across groups. MLA caches a compressed latent that is shared by all heads and expands it into separate keys and values.

followups.q: Is the latent size learned?
followups.a: No. It is a fixed design choice.

topic: CME295 L3: LLMs, MoE, decoding and inference
q: How does speculative decoding speed up generation without changing the output distribution?
plain: Speculative decoding lets a small draft model guess several tokens, then a big model checks them all in one pass. This works because generation is limited by memory speed, not by arithmetic. Checking several tokens in one pass costs about the same as making one. The big model accepts or rejects each guess with a rule that keeps its own output distribution unchanged. When a guess is rejected, generation resumes from that point with a corrected draw. If all guesses are accepted, the big model also gives one extra token for free. For example, with 0.8 acceptance and 4 draft tokens, each big model pass yields about 3.4 tokens.
deep:
Procedure:

1. A small draft model proposes $\gamma$ tokens autoregressively (cheap, since it is small).
2. The target model runs once over the prompt plus the $\gamma$ draft tokens and returns its distributions at all positions, including one extra position after the last draft token.
3. Each draft token is accepted or rejected by a rule that makes the output distribution match the target (next card). On the first rejection, resample that position from a corrected distribution and discard the later draft tokens. If all are accepted, sample one bonus token from the extra position's distribution.

Why one pass costs about the same as one token: at inference you are memory bound, so computation is not the limiting factor, and loading the weights dominates. Verifying several positions at once is nearly free.

Expected speed: with per token acceptance rate $\alpha$ (assumed independent) and $\gamma$ draft tokens, the expected number of tokens per target pass is $(1-\alpha^{\gamma+1})/(1-\alpha)$. For $\alpha=0.8$, $\gamma=4$ this is $3.36$ (the closed form is the standard result from the speculative decoding paper, not derived in the lecture). Output quality is unchanged, because the final distribution equals the target's.
say: Speculative decoding speeds up generation by having a small draft model propose several tokens and a big model verify them all in one forward pass. It works because inference is memory bound, so checking several positions costs about the same as one. The big model accepts or rejects each draft token with a rule that preserves its own distribution, and on a rejection I resample from a corrected distribution and continue from there. If everything is accepted, I get an extra token for free. For example, with a draft of four tokens and acceptance probability 0.8, each big model pass yields about 3.4 tokens. The output quality doesn't change, only the speed.
must_mention: big model verifies them in one pass
memory bound so a pass costs about the same
accept or reject rule preserves the target distribution
bonus token when all are accepted

followups.q: Why is verifying k tokens as cheap as generating one?
followups.a: Inference is memory bound, so reading the weights dominates, and scoring several positions in parallel adds little.

followups.q: What happens on a rejection?
followups.a: Resample that position from a corrected distribution, drop the remaining draft tokens, and continue generating from there.

traps: Saying speculative decoding is an approximation that lowers quality. With the correct rule the distribution is exactly the target's.

topic: CME295 L3: LLMs, MoE, decoding and inference
q: Why does the speculative decoding acceptance rule give exactly the target model's distribution?
plain: The rule is built so that the final token is drawn from the big model's distribution, whatever the draft model says. A draft token is kept with probability equal to the big model's probability divided by the draft's, capped at 1. If the big model likes the token at least as much as the draft, it is always kept. If the draft overrates a token, it is sometimes rejected, which trims the excess. After a rejection, the replacement is drawn from only the leftover probability, where the big model exceeds the draft. Adding the kept and replaced routes for each token gives exactly the big model's probability. For example, big model 0.6, 0.3, 0.1 and draft 0.4, 0.4, 0.2 give final probabilities 0.6, 0.3 and 0.1. The lecture proves it with the law of total probability (adding up the ways an outcome can happen).
deep:
Let $p$ be the target distribution and $q$ the draft distribution at one position. Draw $x\sim q$. Accept it with probability $\min\!\big(1,p(x)/q(x)\big)$. If rejected, draw from the residual

$$
r(x)=\frac{\max(0,\,p(x)-q(x))}{\sum_y\max(0,\,p(y)-q(y))}
$$

Probability that the output equals $x$ (law of total probability over the accept and reject routes):

$$
P(\text{out}=x)=q(x)\min\!\Big(1,\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}\Big)+\Big(1-\sum_y\min(p(y),q(y))\Big)r(x)
$$

The first term is $\min(p(x),q(x))$. The rejection probability is $1-\sum_y\min(p,q)=\sum_y\max(0,p-q)$ because both $p$ and $q$ sum to 1, so the second term is exactly $\max(0,p(x)-q(x))$. Since $\min(p,q)+\max(0,p-q)=p$, the output is $p(x)$.

Numbers: $p=(0.6,0.3,0.1)$, $q=(0.4,0.4,0.2)$. The overall acceptance probability is $\sum\min(p,q)=0.8$, the residual is $(1,0,0)$, and the output probabilities are $0.4+0.2=0.6$, $0.4\times0.75=0.3$ and $0.2\times0.5=0.1$. This is a form of rejection sampling, which the lecture notes some students already know. The extra position after the last draft token gives its distribution for free, so one more token can be sampled from it.
say: I draw a token x from the draft distribution q and accept it with probability min of one and p over q, where p is the target distribution. If I reject, I sample from the leftover distribution, the positive part of p minus q, normalized. Then the probability of outputting x is min of p and q, from the accept path, plus the rejection probability times the leftover, which equals the positive part of p minus q. Those two add up to p of x, so the output is exactly the target distribution. The rejection probability is one minus the sum of min p q, which equals the sum of the positive parts, so the normalization works out.
must_mention: accept with probability min of 1 and p over q
resample from the normalized positive part of p minus q
accept path gives min of p and q
reject path gives the positive part of p minus q

followups.q: Where does the normalizer of the residual come from?
followups.a: The rejection probability, one minus the sum of min of p and q, equals the sum of the positive parts of p minus q because both sum to one.

followups.q: What kind of method is this?
followups.a: A form of rejection sampling with a correction step.

topic: CME295 L3: LLMs, MoE, decoding and inference
q: What is multi token prediction, and how does it relate to speculative decoding?
plain: Multi token prediction trains a model to predict several future tokens at once instead of only the next one. It adds extra output heads on top of the last decoder layer, one for each future position. At generation time, those extra heads act as the draft model, and the main head acts as the checker. So the draft and the target models live inside one network, with no second model to run. The extra heads' guesses are fed back to the main head, which accepts or rejects them. The paper uses a greedy check, so the exact match with the big model's distribution is not guaranteed. For example, 3 extra heads propose 3 future tokens, and each accepted token saves one full pass.
deep:
Multi token prediction is the same idea as speculative decoding with the draft model embedded in the main model. It attaches multiple heads on top of the representation of the last decoder layer. Changes:

- Training: the objective is multi word prediction, not just next word prediction.
- Inference: the extra heads are the draft model, the first (usual next token) head is the target. The draft tokens are fed back to the first head, which accepts or rejects them.
- Acceptance: the paper does this greedily, not with the probability ratio rule. Because the architecture and objective changed, there is no longer the property that the output distribution equals the next token model's, but there is a slight variation of it.

Two things to note from the lecture: the change in the objective function, and that the draft model and the target model sit in the same network, so they do not have to be separated.
say: Multi token prediction trains the model to predict several future tokens at once, by attaching extra output heads on top of the last decoder layer. At inference, those extra heads act as the draft model and the main head acts as the verifier, so I get the speed up of speculative decoding without a second model. The draft tokens are fed back through the main head, which accepts or rejects them. The paper uses a greedy acceptance rule, because the architecture and objective changed, so the exact guarantee of matching the original next token distribution is lost. The key points are the changed training objective and that draft and target live in one model.
must_mention: extra heads on the last decoder layer
heads act as the draft model

followups.q: How does it differ from standard speculative decoding?
followups.a: The draft is built into the same network, and the check is greedy, so the exact distribution guarantee is lost.

followups.q: What changes at training time?
followups.a: The objective predicts several future tokens instead of only the next one.

topic: CME295 L4: LLM training
q: What is transfer learning, and how does it shape the way LLMs are trained?
