Further strong areas in government and services: administrative services managers, compliance officers, medical and health services managers, personal financial advisors and customer service representatives. Also first line supervisors of retail sales workers, non retail sales workers, editing tasks, and research or detective style roles and news analysts.

Variation by duration and modality: models did better on shorter tasks up to a few hours, with a decline on longer tasks, and some models are better on multimodal work while others are better on text.

Underspecified prompts: if you remove context from the prompt, the models do not do as well, a few points lower in win rate, and mostly the model struggles to figure out what to work on. Real work includes a lot of figuring out what needs to be worked on, how context should be used and what should be in the context, which models do not capture on their own. Humans orchestrate what to work on, and the model solves it in certain cases. This links to the METR finding that repository maintainers are much faster than external contractors: real work is context heavy.

Caveat from a class question: the benchmark's expert for software may be closer to repository maintainers, while for industrial or mechanical engineering a decade of experience matters. Takeaway: AI assistance is already cost effective when coupled with human oversight, though different models are stronger on different task types.
say: In GDPval, models were near expert level in occupations like counter clerks, real estate brokers, inventory clerks, purchasing agents, computer systems managers and software developers, and strong in areas like compliance, medical services management, financial advising and customer service. They did better on shorter tasks of up to a few hours. Context is the big caveat. When the prompt was underspecified, win rates fell a few points, mostly because the model couldn't work out what to work on. Real work depends on priorities and context that humans supply, so AI is cost effective mainly with human oversight.
must_mention: near par in clerks, brokers, purchasing, IT managers, software
models struggle to decide what to work on

followups.q: What does average expert mean here?
followups.a: The comparison is to an experienced expert, not the best one in the field.

followups.q: What does the context finding imply?
followups.a: Humans must define the problem and supply context, and the model executes.

traps: Reading near par as models replacing the whole occupation.

topic: CS329A P8: Agentic evaluations
q: What is DeepScholar Bench, and what does it measure?
plain: DeepScholar Bench is a Stanford benchmark for deep research: write the related work section of a paper. The task needs fresh queries, because new papers keep appearing. It uses recent arXiv papers across 22 domains and reruns every month with new papers. Only papers newer than the models' training are used, which avoids data contamination. It scores 3 axes: knowledge synthesis, retrieval quality and verifiability. Knowledge synthesis checks whether the text is coherent and captures the key facts, called nuggets. Retrieval quality checks how relevant and important the retrieved papers are. Verifiability checks whether citations support the claims and whether claims are backed by citations.
deep:
The task is one a classmate requested early on: have AI write the literature review section of a paper. The benchmark asks whether AI can perform deep research synthesis: study a bunch of references, retrieve the relevant information and synthesize the findings into a coherent report with verifiable citations. Industry prototypes include OpenAI Deep Research, Gemini Deep Research, Perplexity, STORM (from Stanford) and OpenScholar, and homework 3 had students build a deep research agent.

Task and data: generate the related work section for academic papers, which requires continuous updates with fresh queries, so there is no staleness. The dataset uses recent arXiv papers with PhD level difficulty across 22 domains, rerun monthly with new papers, so it stays live and avoids data contamination, using only papers posted after the training of a major model.

Three evaluation axes:
1. Knowledge synthesis: is the output well organized and coherent, and does it capture the key facts (the key nuggets)?
2. Retrieval quality: how relevant are the references, how important are the retrieved documents (for example citation counts as a signal of authority), and what is the reference coverage (is it finding the important papers)?
3. Verifiability: do the citations support the claims (citation precision) and are claims backed by citations (claim coverage). One measures precision and the other coverage.

Each metric was validated by humans, with about 70 to 80 percent human agreement.

Why include this benchmark: for real world tasks to be meaningful, models have to use knowledge bases in useful ways, so this is a representative task for that category.
say: DeepScholar Bench, from Stanford, tests deep research: write the related work section of a paper. It uses recent arXiv papers across twenty two domains, rerun monthly with new papers, so it stays live and avoids contamination. It scores three axes. Knowledge synthesis checks coherence and whether key facts, the nuggets, are covered. Retrieval quality checks relevance, importance of the sources and reference coverage. Verifiability checks that citations support the claims and that claims are backed by citations. The metrics were validated with about seventy to eighty percent human agreement.
must_mention: verifiability: citation precision and claim coverage

followups.q: Why a live benchmark?
followups.a: It avoids data contamination and staleness by using only newly posted papers.

followups.q: How were the metrics validated?
followups.a: By human agreement of about 70 to 80 percent.

traps: Evaluating only fluency. The benchmark checks facts, sources and citations too.

topic: CS329A P8: Agentic evaluations
q: What did DeepScholar Bench find about current deep research systems?
plain: In the DeepScholar Bench paper, no existing system scored above 19 percent overall. That leaves lots of headroom, unlike many saturated benchmarks. OpenAI Deep Research did well on synthesis, but almost all systems missed key facts. Retrieval quality was only okay, and document importance was below 12.5 percent for all systems. The DeepScholar baseline reached about 90 percent verifiability precision. Open deep research systems had lower verifiability, despite very fluent writing. Even with a perfect set of sources, models covered only about 50 percent of the key facts. No system excelled at both synthesis quality and verifiability.
deep:
Most benchmarks get saturated: when something is already at 70 or 80 percent there is no headroom. This benchmark is different: none of the existing systems exceeds 19 percent, so it is open for a final project.

Results by axis, from the lecture:
- Knowledge synthesis: OpenAI Deep Research does a pretty good job, but almost all the models consistently miss key facts. The writing is coherent, great English, but it does not cover all the key facts.
- Retrieval quality: overall okayish. All systems currently struggle to find a comprehensive and important set of sources, and document importance is below 12.5 percent in all of them.
- Verifiability: the DeepScholar baseline got up to about 90 percent precision, while open deep research systems have lower verifiability even though they do a really good job writing nice English with extremely coherent synthesis.

Failure modes: not finding comprehensive sources. Even when relevant documents are found they do not always find the foundational papers, which an expert knows from building context and bookmarking the important papers. Agents do a reasonably strong job on relevance but struggle to assess document importance beyond relevance to the context. They also fail to surface essential facts: even given the perfect set of sources (the papers that should have been included), key fact coverage is about 50 percent, and lower without the exact papers. Balancing synthesis quality against verifiability, no system excels at both.

Interpretation: referring to reference data is non trivial in agentic evaluation tasks. A model has less foundational knowledge than an expert, may not extract key information well, and its citation precision and recall may not meet the standard an occupation needs.
say: In the DeepScholar Bench paper, no existing system scored above nineteen percent overall, so there's a lot of headroom. OpenAI Deep Research did well on synthesis, but almost every system missed key facts. Retrieval was only okayish, with document importance below twelve and a half percent for all systems. On verifiability, the DeepScholar baseline reached about ninety percent precision, while some open deep research systems were lower despite very fluent writing. Even given perfect sources, key fact coverage was only about fifty percent, and no system excelled at both synthesis and verifiability.
must_mention: verifiability varies, about 90 percent for the baseline
about 50 percent key fact coverage even with perfect sources

followups.q: Why is fluent writing misleading here?
followups.a: A coherent section can still miss key facts and cite weakly.

followups.q: What would help most?
followups.a: Better source finding, importance assessment and fact extraction with verified citations.

traps: Judging a research agent by how well it writes.

topic: CS329A P8: Agentic evaluations
q: Compare METR, GDPval and DeepScholar Bench: what does each measure, and what does each miss?
plain: METR measures task length, scored automatically, with a single agent and no cost for mistakes or resources. GDPval measures economic value, with well specified, one shot tasks that need tacit knowledge already in the model. It has no back and forth, so a human cannot guide the model to fix its work. DeepScholar Bench measures research synthesis, where finding good sources and verifying claims is the hard part. Research synthesis tasks can take 30 minutes to 8 hours. Models reach about a 50 minute horizon there, but quality may still be poor, around 50 percent success. Each benchmark is a partial view, so you need duration, economic value and synthesis quality metrics. All should be checked against humans who can solve the tasks.
deep:
The lecture's summary across the three benchmarks, and how each differs from real work. Benchmarks are never perfect: they are a representation of what we think is measurable today.

METR (time horizon): automatically scored, no multi agent interaction (single agent tasks), not punishing of mistakes, and no resource constraints on how much can be used. In real work you may have more subjective constraints in how things are scored, you may split a task across multiple agents, and there are resource constraints and costs of mistakes.

GDPval (economic value): the tasks are extremely well specified, all the context the human would have in their head is written into the task, and it is one shot, with no iterative back and forth to fix what the model did. It requires some tacit knowledge to already be in the model. That gap is covered more by the third benchmark.

DeepScholar Bench (research synthesis): models still struggle with finding comprehensive, high quality sources, surfacing key facts and verifying them. A human who is an expert and does this daily is much faster, because the context is in their head. Research synthesis tasks can run from 30 minutes to 8 hours, and the current capability range is about 50 minutes at the horizon, but the quality at this horizon may still be poor, maybe 50 percent success. So even if they look good on the METR plot, they may not be high quality in economic value terms. They require multi step reasoning, comprehensive information gathering and maintaining verifiability while synthesizing, with context engineering over a distributed set of tool calls, as in homework 3.

Conclusion: you need metrics that are duration based, economic value based and synthesis quality based, and you need to validate them against humans who can solve the tasks.
say: Each benchmark is a different slice. METR measures task length, scored automatically, single agent, with no penalty for mistakes or resource limits. GDPval measures economic value on fully specified, one shot tasks that rely on tacit knowledge already in the model, with no iterative feedback. DeepScholar Bench measures research synthesis, where finding sources, extracting key facts and verifying claims is the hard part, and quality is poor even at horizons that look fine on METR. So I'd report duration, economic value and synthesis quality together, and validate each against human experts.
must_mention: METR: automatic scoring, single agent, no mistake cost
research synthesis horizon about 50 minutes but low quality
need several metrics validated against humans

followups.q: What does GDPval assume that real work does not?
followups.a: That all context is in the prompt, and that one shot is enough.

followups.q: Why can METR flatter research tasks?
followups.a: It measures length of task completed, not the quality or verifiability of the result.

traps: Using a single benchmark as a proxy for real world agent value.

topic: CS329A P8: Agentic evaluations
q: What do these benchmarks tell us we know, and do not know, about model capabilities?
plain: Models improved on isolated, well specified tasks, especially in software engineering and machine learning research. They solve hour long tasks there and produce well organized outputs, even if parts are wrong. Confidence is lower on tasks that need a lot of context. Models struggle with ambiguous prompts and do not figure out what to work on. Performance in adversarial environments is not necessarily good. At 95 percent reliability, models are not there yet. There is little evidence yet of generalization beyond software and knowledge work. Finding comprehensive, high quality sources and verifying key facts are still gaps.
deep:
What we know (lecture): models have been improving on isolated, well specified tasks. If you have well specified tasks in domains where models are good, they do a really good job. Software engineering and ML research are two domains with significant progress, perhaps because computer scientists understand those domains better ("we are automating away our own jobs"). Models solve hour long tasks there, and the stronger models generate very well organized outputs even if not all parts are correct.

What we have lower confidence in:
- Tasks that need a lot of context: if the context is not in the prompt, the model does not know what to work on and does not figure out ambiguous prompts.
- Adversarial environments: performance is not necessarily great.
- Reliability: at 95 percent, the models are not quite there.
- Generalization beyond software and knowledge work (knowledge work encompasses a lot of today's digital workloads).
- Finding comprehensive, high quality sources when referencing knowledge bases, surfacing key facts and verifying them, with high accuracy and high coverage.

Closing summary across the three papers: METR's seven month doubling of the horizon at 50 percent reliability, forecast to give month long tasks around 2028 to 2031, is contradicted in some ways by the more linear gain of GDPval win rate over two years, where a 48 percent win rate for some tasks coexists with many categories without high win rates. A lot of GDPval tasks require context or reference data, and DeepScholar shows critical gaps in retrieval and verification. Reliability and error recovery should keep improving, but performance varies by task type, so longer horizons do not automatically mean reliable, high quality outputs.
say: Models clearly improved on isolated, well specified tasks, especially software engineering and machine learning research. They solve hour long tasks there and write well organized outputs, even if parts are wrong. I have lower confidence in tasks that need lots of context, ambiguous prompts, adversarial settings, and ninety five percent reliability. There's also little evidence of generalization beyond software and knowledge work, and models still struggle to find comprehensive sources and verify key facts. So longer horizons don't automatically mean reliable, high quality results.
must_mention: strong on well specified isolated tasks
software engineering and ML research lead
weak on context heavy and ambiguous tasks

followups.q: Why might software and ML research be ahead?
followups.a: They are well specified, checkable domains that the builders understand well.

followups.q: What would you want to see next?
followups.a: Reliability at 95 percent, generalization beyond software, and verified source use.

traps: Extrapolating from software results to all knowledge work.

topic: CS329A P8: Agentic evaluations
q: How is the METR 50 percent success rate computed?
plain: A student asked whether 50 percent means an average success rate or a guarantee on every task. The lecturer says it comes from multiple attempts at each task. Each task gets a success rate: the share of the agent's runs that succeed. Suppose a task has 10 attempts and 5 succeed, so its rate is 50 percent. Points on the plot are these per task success rates, drawn against human time. A student suggested averaging them over the 97 tasks, and the lecturer said that is roughly right. The horizon is read where the fitted curve of success against human time crosses 50 percent. So a 50 percent horizon does not mean each task succeeds half the time.
deep:
Student question: the 50 percent task completion rate, is it an average success rate (say 100 test instances, each tried 10 times, counted and averaged), or is it stricter, requiring at least 50 percent on every task?

Answer: it is multiple attempts for sure, as in the plot with multiple agent runs, counting how many times it completed successfully. With about 97 tasks in the suite, for each task you calculate the success rate of the agent over its attempts, and then, as the student suggests, you average the individual task success rates. The lecturer's agreement is "roughly right": for each horizon they draw points, where the success rate of each point comes from the percentage of attempts that were successful. A 50 percent success rate for one task would mean that 50 percent of the time the agent might come back with a good answer.

How to read the headline: the horizon is where the fitted curve of success rate against human time crosses 50 percent. It is not a statement that every task of that length succeeds half the time. Some tasks of that length succeed almost always and others almost never.

Interview framing: this is a curve fit over per task success probabilities (a logistic style fit in the paper, as I recall, which is background). The unit of analysis is the task, and the success probability per task is estimated from repeated runs, so the number of attempts affects the noise.
say: In METR, each task is attempted multiple times by the agent, and the task's success rate is the share of attempts that succeed. Those per task rates are plotted against how long a human takes, and a curve is fitted. The fifty percent horizon is where the fitted curve crosses fifty percent. So it's not a guarantee that every task of that length succeeds half the time, and it's not an average over all tasks either. Some tasks at that length succeed almost always, and others almost never. A student suggested averaging per task rates, and the lecturer said that was roughly right.
must_mention: horizon is where the fitted curve crosses 50 percent
not a guarantee on each task

followups.q: What is the unit of analysis?
followups.a: The task, with its success probability estimated from repeated runs.

followups.q: Does a 50 percent horizon mean 50 percent per task?
followups.a: No. It is where the fitted curve over many tasks crosses 50 percent.

traps: Reading the horizon as a per task guarantee.

topic: CS329A P8: Agentic evaluations
q: Why is the long tail of tasks hard for models, and where is progress faster?
plain: The lecturer says the first 80 percent of a problem can be far easier than the last 20 percent. Distributed systems is one area where models struggle to get things right. The long tail is partly a data problem and partly a model capability problem. Startups build environments and collect data to cover tasks that are representative. Legal and financial research saw faster adoption and improvement. In very specific areas, such as robotics, whole startups focus on data collection to close the gap. Reliability across the long tail is expected to be extremely challenging. For now, a model that brainstorms with scientists is more useful than one that runs the whole research loop.
deep:
Q and A at the end of the lecture.

Long tail: the lecturer says there will be a long tail of tasks that continue to be challenging for models, including tasks that are not just pull request based. Using the familiar saying, the first 80 percent is easier and the last 20 percent takes much longer. Distributed systems is one area of computer science where it is very hard for the models to get it right.

Why: it is a mix of a data problem and a fundamental model capability problem. Several startups are tackling it by building environments and coming up with representative tasks, and closing the gap in model capabilities for each of these tasks is still challenging. When tasks are brought across categories such as legal research or financial research, those have seen much faster adoption and improvement. When the area is very specific, having enough data and the right model capabilities is hard. In robotics (embodied AI) there is a whole suite of startups going after data collection as the primary hypothesis to close the gap on top of these models.

Outlook given by the lecturer: timelines are moving extremely fast and it is hard to predict one year ahead. Being able to act as an AI scientist, coming up with hypotheses, running experiments and completing the whole loop, is the lecturer's definition of the milestone where models build the next generation of models, and that is not there yet. At this point an AI co scientist, a strong brainstorming partner, has more value. Reliability, and the long tail of reliability, will be extremely challenging. Computer science as a profession is not going away, and reasoning from fundamentals is an important skill, because models need the context that people give them.
say: The long tail is hard because the first eighty percent of a problem is much easier than the last twenty, and distributed systems is an example where models struggle. It's partly a data problem and partly a model capability problem. Startups are building environments and collecting data to cover representative tasks, and areas like legal and financial research have seen faster adoption, while very specific areas like robotics need whole companies built around data collection. The lecturer expects reliability across the long tail to stay extremely challenging, and sees a model that brainstorms with scientists as more useful for now than one that runs the whole research loop.
must_mention: first 80 percent easier than last 20 percent
legal and financial research adopt faster
co scientist more valuable than autonomous scientist for now

followups.q: Which areas improve faster?
followups.a: Categories with clear tasks and data, such as legal and financial research.

followups.q: Why is robotics different?
followups.a: Data is scarce, so startups focus on data collection to close the gap.

traps: Assuming reliability on the long tail will follow automatically from scale.

topic: CS329A P9: Future research areas
q: What did the course cover, in one pass?
plain: The course followed a path from better language models to self improving agents. It began with test time and train time scaling, driven by verifiers, rewards, reinforcement learning and search. Math and coding were the main early testbeds, because answers can be checked. A class on open endedness added exploration, where models explore without only following rewards, for example AlphaEvolve. Then the course built end to end agent workflows with tool use. Multi step tasks also need retrieval and memory, plus better planning and multi step reasoning. Last came evaluation of new models, plus guest lectures on post training, multimodal agents and robotics. The final lecture adds 2 themes: self improvement and the efficiency of intelligence.
deep:
Overview given at the start of the final lecture. The class began with an overview of LLMs and how, over the past year, test time scaling and train time scaling with self improvement techniques have worked, where the fundamental loop is driven by verifiers and feedback from running those verifiers and getting rewards, then using reinforcement learning and even search algorithms to help models hill climb on math and coding. From there came a class on evolutionary strategies and open endedness, where the loop is not driven only by rewards and models are allowed to explore if the exploration space can be defined (AlphaEvolve and similar techniques). Then the course moved to end to end workflows for agents with tool use, as models interact with environments and tools. For tasks that need multiple steps you need knowledge bases, which brings retrieval and memory. As you go toward real world workflows you need better planning and multi step reasoning, which several works covered, then evaluations for the next generation of models and what capabilities would drive them. There were also guest lectures on post training, multimodal agents and robotics, and reasoning, and a speaker on symbolic techniques under the umbrella of tool use, which can add to synthetic data, another current trend.

The framing for this lecture: it organizes key ideas from papers on the self improvement side and on the efficiency side of intelligence, both seen as extremely important directions for the next research areas.
say: The course started with test time and train time scaling, where verifiers and rewards drive reinforcement learning and search so models can hill climb on math and coding. Then a class on open endedness, where models explore without only following rewards, like AlphaEvolve. After that came end to end agent workflows with tool use, retrieval and memory for multi step tasks, and planning and multi step reasoning. The course also covered evaluation of next generation models, plus guest lectures on post training, multimodal agents and robotics. The final lecture adds two themes: self improvement and the efficiency of intelligence.
must_mention: test time and train time scaling with verifiers
end to end workflows with tools

followups.q: What is the core loop of the first half?
followups.a: Verifiers and feedback give rewards, and RL or search hill climbs on them.

followups.q: What did open endedness add?
followups.a: Exploration that is not driven only by rewards.

traps: Describing the course as only about language models. It is about agents.

topic: CS329A P9: Future research areas
q: How does the lecture define an agent, and what goes into an agentic workflow?
plain: An agent generalizes a language model by adding a goal. It interacts with the environment, collects feedback and uses it to correct its steps. So an agent is a system that directs its own process, uses tools and works toward a goal. Language models alone are often not powerful enough to drive a whole goal. So people often handwrite workflows that orchestrate models and tools. A workflow has 6 parts: model calls, verifiers, judge models, tool calls, search and parallel calls. In coding agents, the workflow is increasingly driven by the model itself. To reach a goal, an agent must plan, reason over many steps, correct itself and keep improving.
deep:
Reminder from the first class: an agent is a generalization of an LLM. It has a goal, it interacts with the environment, collects feedback and uses that feedback to correct its steps. Agents are systems that can direct their own processes, use tools and accomplish a goal. In the current paradigm LLMs alone are often not powerful enough to drive toward a full goal (they are getting there), so we often handwrite systems as workflows where you orchestrate LLMs and tools. In some scenarios, such as coding agents, the agentic workflows are driven by the models themselves, which is why this is an exciting time.

How workflows are constructed: you orchestrate LLMs, you orchestrate verifiers because you need some form of reward, you might have LLMs as judges for verification, you might have tool calls, search algorithms, and parallel LLM calls doing this kind of search. Since an agentic workflow is driving toward a goal, it needs the capability to plan and reason over multiple steps, correct itself if it goes in the wrong direction, and keep improving in its capabilities, which is where self improvement comes in.

Course map: reasoning and planning (Parts 1, 5), tools and code (Part 4), verification (Parts 2, 3), search and deep research (Part 7), evaluation (Part 8).
say: An agent generalizes a language model. It has a goal, it interacts with the environment, collects feedback, and uses that feedback to correct its steps, so it's a system that directs its own process and uses tools. Language models alone often can't drive a whole goal, so people handwrite workflows that orchestrate model calls, verifiers for rewards, judge models, tool calls, search and parallel calls. In coding agents the model increasingly drives the workflow itself. Either way, the agent needs to plan, reason over many steps, correct itself and keep improving.
must_mention: directs its own process and uses tools
parts: model calls, verifiers, judges, tools, search, parallel calls

followups.q: What is the difference between a workflow and an agent?
followups.a: A workflow is hand designed orchestration, while an agent directs its own process toward the goal.

followups.q: Where do models already drive the workflow?
followups.a: Coding agents.

traps: Calling any model with a prompt an agent.

topic: CS329A P9: Future research areas
q: What are the three bottlenecks for self improving systems that the lecture highlights?
plain: The lecture names 3 bottlenecks for self improving systems. First, scaling works mostly in narrow areas like math and coding, so generalization is a problem. Reasoning chains must also be diverse enough to keep the loop improving. Second, verification must be reliable, and reasoning chains may need meta verification (checking the checker). Third, training prompts are chosen statically and usually by humans. So the loop needs a way to pick the right data on its own. A second theme is efficiency: how much intelligence you get per unit of cost. Three papers in the first half each address one bottleneck.
deep:
What we learned in the classes: test time scaling, where you improve by having multiple samples and majority voting, and train time scaling, where you use the feedback in the inference loop and get rewards to drive the self improvement loop. Often this is still limited to narrow domains like math and coding. So the first bottleneck: how do you get generalization across domains, and how do you get reasoning chains diverse enough to keep driving the self improvement loop?

Second bottleneck: verification. An important aspect of building self improvement loops continues to be verification: how do you have reliable verification, or meta verification techniques where you verify what went into the reasoning chain?

Third bottleneck: even though we talk about train time scaling, the prompts that go into training these models are selected very statically and require humans to select them. How do you break through the data barrier so that the self improvement loop can pick the right data to drive the loop?

The second half of the lecture focuses on what drives efficiency of intelligence (intelligence per what). The lecture notes that, given how fast the field moves, there may be papers on each of these next time.

Mapping to papers: diversity of reasoning chains (Multiagent Finetuning), verification and meta verification (DeepSeekMath V2), data and task selection (Absolute Zero).
say: The lecture names three bottlenecks. First, scaling mostly works in narrow areas like math and coding, so generalization is a problem, and the reasoning chains need to be diverse enough to keep the loop improving. Second, verification has to be reliable, and reasoning chains may need meta verification, a check on the checker. Third, training prompts are chosen statically, usually by humans, so the loop needs to pick its own data. Each of the first three papers addresses one of these. The other theme is efficiency, meaning intelligence per unit of cost.

followups.q: Which paper addresses each bottleneck?
followups.a: Multiagent Finetuning for diversity, DeepSeekMath V2 for verification, Absolute Zero for data selection.

followups.q: Why is diversity a bottleneck?
followups.a: Without diverse reasoning chains the loop stops improving after a few iterations.

traps: Treating verification as solved because math has final answers.

topic: CS329A P9: Future research areas
q: Why does self improvement from a single model plateau, and what fixes it?
plain: Pretraining compresses internet scale data, and instruction tuning needs costly human preference data. So synthetic data from the model itself is attractive. Iterative self improvement generates solutions, keeps the correct ones (rejection sampling) and fine tunes on them. With only 1 model generating data, the solutions are very similar to each other. Gains then stop after tens of iterations. Pretraining data is diverse because many humans wrote it over a long time. A single model stays low in diversity even at high temperature. The fix proposed is multiple specialized agents, which bring diversity.
deep:
The key idea of the Multiagent Finetuning paper (self improvement with diverse reasoning chains): pretraining compute is a compression of internet scale data, and instruction fine tuning often requires real human data, since you need human preferences to decide what is a good or bad model response. An alternative is data generated by LLMs, often called synthetic data, with iterative fine tuning: generate possible solutions, filter out the incorrect ones (this is called rejection sampling) and fine tune only on the good ones. There are many variants, such as STaR (covered in class), and you can add reasoning chains to the process.

The problem: if a single large language model generates the data, it generates very similar solutions, and the performance increase stops after a few iterations or tens of iterations. This comes down to a lack of diversity. At pretraining scale the data is very diverse, because it was generated over a long time by humans, and that helps performance. But when a single LLM generates outputs for a set of prompts, it does not have very diverse responses, even at high temperatures.

The intuitive solution is to use multiple agents that are specialized in some way and use them to improve diversity: multiple specialized generation agents that produce diverse initial solutions, plus critic agents that evaluate and refine them (next card).
say: Pretraining only compresses internet data and instruction tuning needs expensive human preference data, so I'd generate synthetic data from the model itself: sample solutions, keep the correct ones with rejection sampling, and fine tune on them. With a single model that plateaus after a few tens of iterations, because its solutions are all similar. Pretraining data is diverse because many people wrote it over time, but one model has low diversity even at high temperature. The proposed fix is multiple specialized agents, which bring diversity.
must_mention: single model solutions are too similar
gains stop after tens of iterations

followups.q: Does a higher temperature fix it?
followups.a: Not enough. A single model stays low in diversity even at high temperature.

followups.q: What is STaR's relation?
followups.a: It is a variant of this filter and fine tune loop.

traps: Assuming more iterations always keep improving a single model.

topic: CS329A P9: Future research areas
q: How does multiagent finetuning work?
plain: The method trains 2 kinds of specialized agents: generation agents and critic agents. Generation agents are fine tuned from the same base model and produce diverse initial answers. In debate rounds, each generation agent summarizes the other agents' answers and uses that to write an updated answer. Critic agents then critique the updated answers and select the best one. Having several agents gives majority voting for free, plus diversity. Generation agents are fine tuned on outputs that match the majority vote. Critic agents are fine tuned on trajectories where a wrong answer was corrected during debate. A cheap version just uses different existing models, which also gives varied answers.
deep:
Agents: generation agents (the lecture's generator models are fine tuned from the same base model) produce a lot of diverse initial solutions, while critic agents evaluate and refine the solutions. Both are specialists.

Procedure step by step: each generation agent produces an initial answer. Then there is debate over multiple rounds: in the subsequent rounds each generation agent gets a summary of all other agents' responses and uses it in generating its next response. The critic agent then critiques the updated set of answers. So the loop is: initial responses from each generation agent, a summary across all agents (either by a model or by simply concatenating the responses), the critic's critique added to the input, a second round where all models produce updated answers, majority voting on top, and again a summary, continuing like a debate. The main difference from critique of a single agent's response is that you critique multiple agents' responses and summarize across them.

What it enables: diversity even at the generation stage, before critiquing, and majority voting for free just by having multiple agents, assuming they are trained slightly differently.

Training data for each role: over iterations, take outputs and filter for a match with the majority vote, then supervised fine tune generation models on those prompt and response pairs. Critic models take the updated answers and select the best one, and are fine tuned on a mix of trajectories where answers are correct at the start and ones corrected during the debate, so the critic learns to contrast correct and incorrect answers. Those trajectories can also fine tune different critics. A naive version is to use different models, which people do in practice, since different models and prompts give different responses.
say: Multiagent finetuning trains two kinds of specialists from the same base model: generation agents and critic agents. Each generation agent writes an initial answer. Then in debate rounds each one summarizes the other agents' answers and writes an updated answer, and the critic agents critique the updated set and pick the best. Having several agents gives majority voting for free and keeps answers diverse. Generation agents are fine tuned on outputs that match the majority vote, and critics on trajectories where a wrong answer got corrected during the debate. A cheap version just uses different existing models.
must_mention: debate rounds with summaries of other agents
generators fine tuned on majority matching outputs
critics fine tuned on corrected trajectories

followups.q: How are summaries made?
followups.a: By a model, or by simply concatenating the other agents' responses.

followups.q: What is the cheap alternative?
followups.a: Use several different existing models, which also gives varied answers.

traps: Thinking all agents are different base models. They are fine tuned from the same base.

q: What did multiagent finetuning show about diversity and accuracy?
plain: The plots show fine tuning iterations on the x axis. The y axis is either negative log likelihood, a proxy for performance, or embedding dissimilarity, a measure of diversity. Higher embedding dissimilarity means more diverse answers. With multiagent fine tuning, two open source models kept improving over iterations, and Llama 3 responded more. The answers stayed diverse as training went on. On math, tested with 3 open source models, multiagent fine tuning kept improving over several rounds. With single agent fine tuning, accuracy collapsed or stopped improving. It also helped on GSM8K (grade school math), a nearby task, so the gains generalize.
deep:
The key metric: the x axis is how many iterations of fine tuning the model has gone through, and the y axis is either the negative log likelihood or the embedding dissimilarity. The negative log likelihood is a proxy for performance. For embedding dissimilarity, the higher the value, the more diverse the answers.

Left plot: for two open source models, when they go through multiagent fine tuning, they can continue to increase performance, and Llama 3 seems more responsive to the technique. Right plot (the more interesting one): as they go through the process, the responses stay quite diverse. This is over math as the dataset.

Accuracy: they tried it on math with three open source models (they used open source because they were fine tuning). With multiagent techniques they continued to see improvements across multiple steps of fine tuning, while for single agent fine tuning the accuracy collapses or does not continue to improve. They also show it is not only in domain: in adjacent domains like GSM8K the fine tuned agents show higher performance, so it generalizes beyond the datasets they were trained on. The lecturer notes it is an older piece of work, so the absolute numbers are not high.

Takeaway: if we want self improvement, the reasoning chains used to drive it need to be diverse in some way, and one way to generate them is to have multiple models or agents produce the chains.

With multiagent fine tuning, two open source models kept improving across iterations, with Llama 3 more responsive, and the answers stayed diverse. On math with three open source models, multiagent fine tuning kept improving over several rounds, while single agent fine tuning collapsed or stalled. It also improved GSM8K, a nearby task, so it generalizes. The numbers are from older models, so the trend is what matters.

followups.a: How different the embeddings of the generated answers are.

topic: CS329A P9: Future research areas
q: Why is checking only the final answer not enough for theorem proving, and why do language model judges fail?
plain: Most reinforcement learning gives a reward of 1 when the final answer matches the ground truth. That has saturated benchmarks such as AIME (American Invitational Mathematics Examination) and other math tests. But a correct answer can come from incorrect reasoning. Theorem proving needs rigorous step by step derivation, which a final answer does not show. Models trained on quantitative reasoning often write proofs that are mathematically invalid. Asked to judge them, they often say the invalid proofs are valid. So using a language model as a judge does not work well here. Expert humans can spot reasoning gaps and steps that do not follow, but experts are scarce.
deep:
Verification is quite hard for model outputs. Typically you only look at the outcome: for a math problem or a theorem proof you look at the final outcome and use an outcome reward model: does it match the ground truth, then it verifies. The question from the verification lecture: what happens if the reasoning chains are wrong, will that lead the model astray or cause a performance gap at the end? Process reward models are also quite hard to build.

Why final answer rewards fall short for proofs: the current reinforcement learning approach assumes the final answer matches the ground truth, which is how the rewards are created. This has enabled saturation of multiple benchmarks like AIME and other math related ones, but often, even when you have the correct answer, you might not have the correct reasoning. If you want models to get better at theorem proving, you need rigorous step by step derivation, which the final output does not give you.

Why LLM as a judge fails here: large language models are often trained on quantitative reasoning, so the proofs they generate might be mathematically invalid, and if you ask them to verify, they will claim the incorrect proofs are valid. Expert humans looking at proofs can reason about the area and say the proof has issues: the next step does not follow from the last, or there are reasoning gaps in the proof.

This motivates DeepSeekMath V2: train verifiers that find issues in proofs without a reference solution, and add a meta verifier (next cards). It is a recent paper that tries to show that, at least in theorem proving, automated self verification loops are possible.
say: Most RL rewards a model when its final answer matches the ground truth. That has saturated benchmarks like AIME, but a correct answer can come from incorrect reasoning, and theorem proving needs rigorous step by step derivation that a final answer doesn't show. Language model judges also fail here. Models that were trained on quantitative reasoning write invalid proofs and then tend to judge incorrect proofs as valid. Expert humans can spot reasoning gaps and steps that don't follow, but experts are scarce, which motivates training verifiers that find issues without a reference solution.

followups.a: Step level judgments, but those are hard to build.

topic: CS329A P9: Future research areas
q: How does DeepSeekMath V2 build self verification with a meta verifier?
plain: DeepSeekMath V2 trains verifiers instead of only reward models. Humans first identify issues in proofs without any reference solution. Those labels train models to find issues in a proof and to improve it. The architecture has 3 parts: a generator, a verifier and a meta verifier. The generator writes proofs, and the verifier lists issues and scores each proof between 0 and 1. The meta verifier checks whether the verifier's issues really exist and whether the score follows from them. A good verifier improves the generator, and a better generator writes harder proofs that improve the verifier. After a seed of human labels, labeling can be automated, so humans are not the bottleneck.
deep:
What DeepSeekMath V2 proposes: instead of only training reward models, train verifiers, meta verifiers in effect. Humans identify issues in the proofs without any reference solutions, and based on that LLMs are trained to identify issues in a proof and improve on them. You then have a model that can critique proofs itself.

Architecture: as in train time scaling systems there is a generator (a model producing proofs) and a verifier (identifying issues). What DeepSeekMath V2 adds is the meta verifier, which reviews the verifier's analysis for whether it makes sense or whether there are issues with it. The verifier is trained to take the issues and score the proofs on a scale (the captions say 0.5 and 1, most likely a scale of 0, 0.5 and 1). The verifier then improves the generator, and the generator produces harder proofs which in turn improve the verifier. It becomes a loop. Once you seed the data for finding incorrect proofs, you can automate that labeling, so you do not rely only on humans identifying issues once the meta verifier starts to learn.

Meta verification in detail: verifiers can give a correct score when the reasoning is incorrect, for example by fabricating errors. Meta verification evaluates the analysis of the issues: do the identified issues actually exist, and does the score follow from the issues? Experts annotate the quality of this evaluation. In the lecture's picture, reasoning chains sit under an LLM as a judge that identifies issues, and the meta verifier asks whether those issues really exist. Just adding this block improves the quality of the verification.
say: DeepSeekMath V2 trains a verifier that finds issues in proofs without any reference solution, using human issue labels to start. The architecture has three parts. The generator writes proofs. The verifier lists issues and scores the proof between zero and one. And the meta verifier reviews the verifier's analysis, checking whether the named issues really exist and whether the score follows from them, which cuts fabricated errors. A better verifier improves the generator, and harder proofs improve the verifier, so it's a loop. Once seeded, labeling can be automated.
must_mention: verifier finds issues without reference solutions
meta verifier checks that issues exist and the score follows
verifier and generator improve each other
automated labeling after a human seed

followups.q: What does the meta verifier prevent?
followups.a: Fabricated issues, where a verifier invents errors or scores a wrong proof as right.

followups.q: Where do the first labels come from?
followups.a: Human experts annotating issues in proofs.

traps: Thinking the meta verifier checks the proof itself. It checks the verifier's analysis.

topic: CS329A P9: Future research areas
q: What did DeepSeekMath V2 achieve, and what is the general recipe?
plain: The DeepSeekMath V2 paper builds on a DeepSeek V3 base model and trains with GRPO (group relative policy optimization). It was tested on IMO (International Mathematical Olympiad) style problems. In 8 iterations of the generate and verify loop, the proof score kept climbing. Best of 32 picks the best of 32 proofs, and it reached almost 42 percent on the 2024 IMO shortlist. This suggests promise if you can find issues in reasoning chains and nudge the model to fix them. The recipe has 3 parts: verifiers that find issues without references, a meta verifier, and a generator incentive. The meta verifier reduces made up issues, and the generator is rewarded for quality through deliberate reasoning. The limit is that it works where verification is easier, not in every domain.
deep:
Setup: the RL loop is often built on top of GRPO, and here it is built on top of DeepSeek V3 base models. The generate and verify loop was benchmarked on IMO problems and a second contest set (the captions name it unclearly). The lecture mentions a Gemini version presented by a guest lecturer, and this is the open source version released recently.

Results: in eight iterations, just with the iterative loop, the proof score continues to climb. With best at 32, meaning you pick the best out of 32 generated proofs, the score gets to almost 42 percent on the IMO shortlist of 2024. This is quite promising as a hill climbing technique and suggests there is promise if you identify the issues in the reasoning chains and nudge the model toward correcting them.

Insights: the best proofs achieve higher verification scores, the generator can learn to differentiate higher quality proofs from flawed proofs, and the self verification as a result gives a better improvement loop. Verification can be a bottleneck, and this is one way to break it.

General recipe if you want to apply it to other areas: (1) if you have LLM based verifiers, find a way for them to identify issues without reference solutions, (2) add an extra block, meta verification, to reduce the chance of hallucinated issues identified by the verifier, and (3) add an incentive for the generator to maximize quality through deliberate reasoning. Self verification starts to break the verification bottleneck if you can make it more automated end to end. It is still limited to domains where verification is easier rather than harder.
say: DeepSeekMath V2 builds on a DeepSeek V3 base model with GRPO. In eight iterations of the generate and verify loop the proof score kept climbing, and with best of thirty two, picking the best of thirty two generated proofs, it reached almost forty two percent on the 2024 IMO shortlist. The general recipe has three parts: verifiers that find issues without reference solutions, a meta verifier that reduces hallucinated issues, and an incentive for the generator to reason deliberately. The limit is that it works where verification is feasible, so it's not a universal fix.

best of 32 reaches almost 42 percent on IMO shortlist 2024

followups.a: Pick the highest scoring proof out of 32 generated ones.

topic: CS329A P9: Future research areas
q: What is Absolute Zero, and what problem does it address?
plain: Absolute Zero lets a model propose its own training tasks and then solve them. Today's training stack uses human curated reasoning traces or expert written question and answer pairs. Math needs math experts, olympiad problems need olympiad experts, and coding needs strong programmers. As models pass human level, finding more experts and tasks becomes a limit. Absolute Zero goes to the other extreme: it needs no human written prompts. The model proposes tasks at the edge of what it has learned. It focuses on coding, with 3 kinds of tasks that can be checked by running code. The idea is still new, and it works in domains where verification is available.
deep:
A very interesting paper that has not seen much use yet: have the models propose the set of tasks that they should train on, just at the edge of what they have learned. The current AI training stack either uses human curated reasoning traces (for the supervised learning stage), or, for reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, expects experts to curate question and answer pairs. That requires math experts for math, IMO experts for IMO problems, and strong software coders for coding. As models continue to surpass human intelligence, the ability to find more and more experts and such tasks becomes limiting.

The proposal, still very new: a single model can both propose tasks and then solve them, which goes to the other extreme of not needing an external source of data, so no human generated prompts to climb on. It is feasible in certain domains. The paper focuses on coding and constructs three types of tasks (abduction, deduction and induction).

Student question on environments: the lecturer said the point of environments in the current generation of models is that they are proxies for real world tasks. In the narrow intelligence era you could create simulations for games, used as environments for toy tasks. The real question is what set of tasks you want to represent, and whether an environment, built by agents or by software, is a reasonable proxy for how the model will interact with the real world to get feedback. For gaming the space is finite, so it is easy to represent in code.
say: Absolute Zero lets one model both propose the tasks it trains on and solve them. The motivation is that today's stack needs human curated traces or expert written question and answer pairs, so math needs math experts, olympiad problems need olympiad experts, coding needs strong programmers, and as models surpass humans those experts become the limit. Absolute Zero needs no human written prompts. It proposes tasks at the edge of what it has learned, and it focuses on coding, where tasks can be checked by running code. It works where verification is available.

human curated data and experts are a bottleneck
tasks at the edge of what it has learned

followups.q: Why coding?
followups.a: Tasks and answers can be verified by running code.

followups.q: What is an environment for?
followups.a: It is a proxy for real world tasks, so the question is whether the proxy reflects real interaction.

topic: CS329A P9: Future research areas
q: What are the three task types in Absolute Zero, and how do proposer and solver interact?
plain: Absolute Zero builds 3 types of coding tasks: deduction, abduction and induction. In the proposal stage, the model creates a task of one type. A reward decides which tasks make sense to keep. In the solution stage, the model solves the task, and the answer is verified with an accuracy reward. Both rewards give a joint update to the same model, not a one sided update. The environment, here a code executor, runs programs to get outputs. In the lecture's description, deduction takes a program and an input and gets the output from running it. Induction samples an existing program, makes new inputs and a short description of what it does, and checks the result.
deep:
Overview from the lecture: in the proposal stage the model constructs tasks based on the task types and a reward selects which tasks make sense. In the solution stage it verifies and gives an accuracy reward. This yields a joint update on the model, as opposed to one sided updates.

How the proposer proposes, in the coding paradigm: deduction tasks generate a program and an input, and the environment executes the program to get an output. The lecturer says abduction tasks are similar to deduction (the model generates the program and inputs and the environment computes outputs), and induction tasks are different: the model samples an existing program, generates new inputs for it plus a natural language message describing the function, and the environment executes it and decides whether this is going in the right direction. The proposer is also conditioned on past generated examples that are explicitly prompted in, to promote diversity.

Background, not stated this way in the lecture (my recollection of the paper): deduction means predicting the output given a program and an input, abduction means inferring a plausible input given a program and its output, and induction means synthesizing a program given input and output examples (with a description). The lecture's wording blurs abduction and deduction, so check the paper for exact definitions.

Why a code environment: the executor gives exact outputs, which makes the tasks verifiable and the answers checkable, and the three types cover forward execution, backward inference and program synthesis. The joint update trains one model in two roles, which is why the lecture compares the proposer and solver to a mildly adversarial game that still helps both.
say: Absolute Zero builds three kinds of coding tasks: deduction, abduction and induction. In the proposal stage the model creates a task, and a reward decides which tasks are worth keeping. In the solution stage the same model solves the task and gets an accuracy reward after verification. Both feed a joint update of one model. The environment is a code executor that runs programs to compute outputs, so everything is checkable. As I understand the paper, deduction predicts an output from a program and input, abduction infers an input, and induction synthesizes a program from examples, and I'd check the exact definitions.
must_mention: proposal stage with a task reward
solution stage with an accuracy reward

followups.q: Why is the update joint?
followups.a: One model plays proposer and solver, and both rewards update it.

followups.q: What keeps proposals diverse?
followups.a: The proposer is conditioned on past tasks from a buffer.

traps: Stating the three task definitions as certain. The lecture's wording is loose.

topic: CS329A P9: Future research areas
q: How does Absolute Zero reward the proposer?
plain: The proposer is rewarded for making tasks of the right difficulty. Each proposed task is given to the solver, and the solver's success rate is measured. If the success rate is 0, the proposer gets reward 0. If the success rate is above 0, the proposer gets 1 minus the average success rate. So very easy tasks earn almost nothing, and impossible tasks earn nothing. Moderate tasks, where the solver sometimes succeeds and sometimes fails, earn the most. As the solver improves, the proposer must propose harder tasks to keep earning reward. The proposer is conditioned on past tasks to keep proposals diverse.
deep:
How tasks are selected: each generated task is passed to the solver and its success rate is measured. If the success rate is zero, the proposer gets a zero reward. If the success rate is non zero, the reward is one minus the average success rate. With $\hat p$ the average success rate of the solver on the task:
$$
r_{\text{propose}}=\begin{cases}0, & \hat p=0\\ 1-\hat p, & \hat p>0\end{cases}
$$
(A task the solver always solves, $\hat p=1$, also earns $0$.) The kind of tasks you want are not trivial and not impossible, so there is some ability to keep learning: tasks of moderate difficulty where the solver sometimes succeeds and sometimes fails. Worked example (computed here): $\hat p=0.25$ earns $0.75$, $\hat p=0.75$ earns $0.25$.

The goal of the proposer is to generate tasks of optimal difficulty at the current set of model weights, and as the model becomes more capable the proposer should learn to propose harder problems. The lecturer compares this to game theory: the proposer and solver are slightly adversarial, but overall they help each other improve.

Why this shape: the reward peaks at hard but solvable tasks, which is the learnability idea behind curriculum learning. It also mirrors a point from Part 6: GRPO style updates need a spread of outcomes, since groups where everything succeeds or everything fails give no gradient. A learnability reward targets exactly the tasks that give signal.

Diversity: the proposer is conditioned on past generated examples, explicitly prompted in, to promote diversity (see the buffer card).
say: The proposer's reward is based on learnability. Each proposed task goes to the solver, and I measure the solver's success rate. If the success rate is zero, the proposer gets zero. Otherwise it gets one minus the average success rate. So impossible tasks earn nothing, trivial tasks earn almost nothing, and moderate tasks, where the solver sometimes succeeds and sometimes fails, earn the most. As the solver gets better, the proposer has to propose harder tasks to keep earning. It's a mildly adversarial game that still helps both, and it targets tasks that give a learning signal.
must_mention: solver success rate measured per task
zero reward if the solver never succeeds
moderate difficulty tasks earn the most
proposer must get harder as the solver improves

followups.q: What reward does a task the solver always solves earn?
followups.a: Zero, since one minus a success rate of 1 is zero.

followups.q: Why is this like curriculum learning?
followups.a: Task difficulty tracks the solver's current ability.

traps: Rewarding the proposer for the hardest tasks. Impossible tasks earn nothing.

topic: CS329A P9: Future research areas
q: How does Absolute Zero keep proposed tasks valid, and how does it build a curriculum?
plain: Self made tasks could be garbage, so they are validated before training. In coding, the system executes each task and runs 3 checks: program integrity, safety and repeatability. Repeatability means running the same inputs several times and getting identical outputs. Each valid task is stored in a buffer as a triplet of program, input and output. The buffer also tracks how often the model succeeds or fails on each task. The proposer samples examples from the buffer, which helps diversity. Over time this acts as a curriculum, with tasks that evolve as the model improves. These checks stop the proposer from hacking the reward with garbage tasks.
deep:
Since the model generates tasks, you must make sure they are valid tasks. In the coding abstraction you can run a program integrity check: execute the tasks and see whether there are errors. You can do safety checks. You can also run the inputs multiple times and check that you get exactly the same outputs, because in code that is possible. The proposed task is validated before it goes into the training pipeline, which is one way to make sure the proposer does not hack the reward and come up with garbage tasks.

Buffer: for every seed triplet (the program, the input and the output) you add it to the task buffer, and the proposer can sample references from the buffer. A record is kept of how many times the model succeeds or fails on each task. This leads to a curriculum that evolves over time.

Why it matters: on coding benchmarks this lets you hill climb despite not having human curated data. Humans can generate a lot of coding data, but after a while synthetic data, here generated in the loop at the task level, takes over. A related point from the earlier Q and A: for games the environment is easy to simulate, while for real tasks the question is whether the environment is a reasonable proxy.

Interview framing: any self play data loop needs three guards. A validity check on generated items, a memory of past items for diversity and curriculum, and a difficulty signal from the solver. Without validity checks the proposer exploits the reward.
say: Because the model writes its own tasks, they have to be validated before training. In coding, the system executes each task and runs checks for program integrity, safety, and repeatability, meaning the same inputs give identical outputs on repeated runs. Valid tasks go into a buffer as triplets of program, input and output, with counts of how often the model succeeds or fails on each. The proposer samples examples from that buffer, which promotes diversity and gives a curriculum that evolves as the model improves. These checks keep the proposer from hacking the reward with garbage tasks.
must_mention: buffer of program, input, output triplets

followups.q: Why check repeatability?
followups.a: Tasks with nondeterministic outputs would give noisy or wrong rewards.

followups.q: What does the buffer give besides memory?
followups.a: Diversity through sampled references and a curriculum through success statistics.

traps: Training on proposed tasks without validating them.

topic: CS329A P9: Future research areas
q: What did Absolute Zero achieve, and what behaviors emerged?
plain: Absolute Zero reached state of the art on coding benchmarks without any human curated prompts. It outperformed models trained on tens of thousands of expert examples. The complexity of proposed programs increased over time. The diversity of programs and answers also improved when the loop was set up correctly. The proposer made harder tasks as training progressed. The 2 roles, proposer and solver, are slightly adversarial, like a game, but they help each other improve. Training only on self proposed code tasks still gave strong results on coding and math benchmarks. Larger models got bigger gains than smaller ones.
deep:
What they show: state of the art results on coding benchmarks even though there was no human curated data on the prompt side, outperforming models trained on tens of thousands of expert examples. The lecturer frames it as a play on synthetic data, generated in the loop at the task level.

Emerging behaviors: the complexity metrics increase over time, which is expected if the proposer keeps increasing the difficulty of what it is learning. The diversity of programs and answers also improves when the loop is set up correctly, and the proposer increasingly generates more difficult tasks as training progresses. In some ways it is like game theory: the proposer and solver are slightly adversarial, but overall help each other improve.

Takeaways: the task selection problem, which tasks the models run their self improvement loop on, should not be bottlenecked on human data, because otherwise you are bottlenecked on human experts, as long as you have some form of verification. You also need some ability to do curriculum learning, and this technique relies on that. Even though the model only hill climbs on self proposed code tasks, it sees strong performance on both coding and math benchmarks, which the lecturer calls surprising but explainable from other results in the field. Larger models get bigger gains relative to smaller ones, a pattern the class also saw in SWiRL.

Caveat: the lecture reports the headline qualitatively and gives no numbers, so check the paper for the benchmarks and margins.
say: Absolute Zero reached state of the art on coding benchmarks with no human curated prompts, and it outperformed models trained on tens of thousands of expert examples. As training went on, the complexity of the proposed programs rose and the diversity of programs and answers improved, because the proposer kept making harder tasks. The proposer and solver are slightly adversarial, like a game, but they help each other. Training only on self proposed coding tasks also helped on math, and larger models gained more. The lecture gives no numbers, so I'd check the paper.

beat models trained on tens of thousands of expert examples
helps math too, larger models gain more
